editorial.title: Siding replacement cost in Cincinnati, OH
editorial.description: What drives siding replacement cost in Cincinnati: wall area, material, removal, repairs and trim, with a dated national benchmark and city permit guidance.
editorial.focus: Choose a roofing or storm restoration service, or begin a siding project with its material and installation details in view.

hero.title: Siding replacement cost in Cincinnati, OH
hero.description: Siding replacement cost in Cincinnati comes down to wall area, material, removal and what is found underneath. Consumer Reports, citing the 2025 Cost vs. Value report, gives national averages of nearly $18,000 for vinyl and above $21,000 for fiber cement. Those are national benchmarks, not Cincinnati prices or Roof King quotes. Your price comes from measuring your walls and itemizing the work.

faq.title: Siding cost questions for Cincinnati homeowners

items.question: How much does siding replacement cost in Cincinnati?

children.text: Consumer Reports cites national averages of nearly $18,000 for vinyl and above $21,000 for fiber cement, based on the 2025 Cost vs. Value report. These are not Cincinnati prices or Roof King quotes. A measured estimate prices your walls, materials, removal and repairs.

items.question: Do I need a siding permit in Cincinnati?

children.text: Generally not for replacement siding on a one-, two- or three-family detached dwelling inside city limits, under the city guide. Historic properties, different building types and other jurisdictions need separate checks.

items.question: What changes in a Cincinnati historic district?

children.text: A Certificate of Appropriateness may be needed even when a building permit is not. District guidelines can affect material, profile and color. Get the required approval before ordering.

items.question: Is replacing one elevation cheaper?

children.text: The total is often lower because there is less wall to replace. Matching faded or discontinued panels is the trade-off. Compare new samples against the existing walls.

items.question: Does removal add to the price?

children.text: Yes. Layers, haul-away and disposal affect the total. Agree how repairs to exposed sheathing and flashing are documented, priced and approved.

items.question: Can I price siding from floor area?

children.text: No. Floor area does not measure gables, tall walls, additions and openings. Measure each exterior elevation and the detail work around it.

items.question: Can I finance the project?

children.text: Three- and five-year options, with payments as low as $47 on qualifying projects, are available subject to lender approval and applicable terms. Compare financing separately from the project price.

sections.title: Compare siding materials and installation costs

children.text: Vinyl profiles and finishes have their own accessory and attachment systems. Compare the selected panel, corner and opening details, and whether a particular insulation component is included. Standard vinyl and insulated products should not be treated as the same specification.

Engineered wood combines a wood-based siding appearance with product-specific finishing and installation requirements. The estimate needs to identify the finish, trim and treatment of cut edges and connections for the chosen product.

Fiber cement offers different profiles and finish choices, with its own handling, fastening and detailing requirements. Compare the complete installation rather than assuming a material category comes with one universal price. The
siding materials guide
explains these options further.

sections.title: What adds to a siding replacement quote?

cards.title: Old siding removal and concealed wall repairs

children.text: Removal exposes the wall beneath the old siding. Deteriorated sheathing or trim, unresolved water entry and incomplete flashing may need attention before the new finish is installed. Ask how those findings will be photographed, priced and approved. A new panel cannot correct a concealed wall problem that remains untreated.

cards.title: Window trim, corners, soffits and fixtures

children.text: Corners, window and door trim, roof-to-wall transitions, soffit or fascia work, fixture removal and reinstallation, and cleanup all affect the work. Identify what is included and what will remain. If painting or gutter work is separate, record the boundary and sequence so the finished exterior is coordinated.

cards.title: Like-for-like siding or a redesigned exterior

children.text: A like-for-like replacement with limited trim changes differs from a project that introduces new accent areas, extensive opening details or wall repairs. Both may cover similar wall areas. The useful comparison lists the material, preparation and finish work before the total. Approved measured pricing is needed to turn either approach into a project budget.

sections.title: What your written siding estimate should list

children.text: Compare proposals covering the same work before comparing totals. Your estimate should name:

expectedBlocks: Siding replacement cost in Cincinnati comes down to wall area, material, removal and what is found underneath. Consumer Reports, citing the 2025 Cost vs. Value report, gives national averages of nearly $18,000 for vinyl and above $21,000 for fiber cement. Those are national benchmarks, not Cincinnati prices or Roof King quotes. Your price comes from measuring your walls and itemizing the work.

Vinyl profiles and finishes have their own accessory and attachment systems. Compare the selected panel, corner and opening details, and whether a particular insulation component is included. Standard vinyl and insulated products should not be treated as the same specification.

Engineered wood combines a wood-based siding appearance with product-specific finishing and installation requirements. The estimate needs to identify the finish, trim and treatment of cut edges and connections for the chosen product.

Fiber cement offers different profiles and finish choices, with its own handling, fastening and detailing requirements. Compare the complete installation rather than assuming a material category comes with one universal price. The siding materials guide explains these options further.

Removal exposes the wall beneath the old siding. Deteriorated sheathing or trim, unresolved water entry and incomplete flashing may need attention before the new finish is installed. Ask how those findings will be photographed, priced and approved. A new panel cannot correct a concealed wall problem that remains untreated.

Corners, window and door trim, roof-to-wall transitions, soffit or fascia work, fixture removal and reinstallation, and cleanup all affect the work. Identify what is included and what will remain. If painting or gutter work is separate, record the boundary and sequence so the finished exterior is coordinated.

A like-for-like replacement with limited trim changes differs from a project that introduces new accent areas, extensive opening details or wall repairs. Both may cover similar wall areas. sections.title: How we assess siding damage

children.text: An inspection separates damage to the siding from a problem behind it. These are the three areas we check.
Call for an inspection when you notice:
Buckled, warped or loose courses, or panels that have slipped out of place
Cracks, holes or broken corners after hail or impact
Exposed housewrap or sheathing where a panel is missing
Staining, soft trim or peeling paint near openings
Gaps at corners or where siding meets the roof
Uneven fading and patches that no longer match
Some signs involve the panel itself; staining near a window can start with failed flashing behind it. The inspection is about finding which.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace siding in Columbus?

children.text: Yes, inside city limits. Columbus lists replacement siding as requiring a building permit without plan review. State who applies in the agreement; other jurisdictions set their own requirements.

items.question: Can you replace siding on one side of the house?

children.text: Often. End new work at a corner, trim board or material change. A matching color name may still look different beside aged panels, so compare samples outside.

items.question: How long does siding replacement take?

children.text: Wall area, stories, layers to remove, hidden damage and weather all affect the sequence. Define the product and repairs before setting the expected schedule.

items.question: Will new siding lower energy bills?

children.text: That depends on the installed assembly. Insulated vinyl or a separate insulation layer changes the wall differently from a standard siding panel. Name the actual product and documented insulation value in the estimate.

items.question: Does insurance pay for storm-damaged siding?

children.text: Coverage depends on your policy and the insurer’s findings. Roof King documents the siding, trim and roof edge for the repair discussion.
Storm damage documentation

items.question: What does the workmanship warranty cover?

children.text: Our 5-year workmanship warranty covers installation under the written project terms. Product defects are addressed by the manufacturer’s warranty; storm damage is considered separately.

items.question: Can I finance siding replacement?

children.text: Three- and five-year options are available, with payments as low as $47 on qualifying projects. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms. Compare the cash price, APR, fees and total repayment.

sections.title: How the wall is prepared for new siding

children.text: Removal exposes the wall and connections the new cladding will depend on.

Old siding can hide soft sheathing, deteriorated trim and gaps in the weather barrier, especially below windows and near the base of walls. Record findings, obtain approval for the repair price and correct damaged components before the wall is covered again.

Water behind siding must be directed outside. Lap the barrier and integrate window and door flashing so water sheds over it rather than behind it. New cladding alone does not fix a leaking opening; identify any separate window or door repair in the estimate.

Where siding meets a lower roof, masonry or a deck, the connection needs appropriate flashing and the selected product’s clearances. Sealant alone cannot replace these details. Coordinate roofing and cladding before either covers the connection.

opening.title: Residential Gutter Installation in Columbus

children.text: The roofline determines how the gutter system needs to collect water. The roof area, valleys, corners and pitch influence where runoff collects. The gutter profile, outlet positions and downspouts need to work together so water moves off the house instead of spilling behind the fascia or across a walkway.

We review the condition of the roof edge and discuss the layout of each gutter run. If fascia or adjacent trim is deteriorated, that needs to be addressed before a new gutter is fastened in place. The written proposal should identify the materials, attachment method, downspout locations and any preparation or removal work.

items.question: How do I know whether to repair or replace my gutters?

children.text: A localized joint, outlet or hanger issue may be repairable. Multiple failing sections, corrosion, widespread sagging or damaged supporting materials can make replacement more sensible. The condition of the existing system matters more than its age alone.

items.question: Are seamless gutters completely leak-free?

children.text: No. Seamless construction reduces joints along straight runs, but corners, end caps and outlets still require connections. Installation details and maintenance remain important.

items.question: Will larger gutters stop overflowing?

children.text: Not necessarily. Blocked outlets, poor slope, insufficient downspout capacity or discharge problems can still cause overflow. The whole drainage route needs to be evaluated.

items.question: Do gutter guards eliminate cleaning?

children.text: No. Guards can reduce certain debris entry, but the gutter, outlets and downspouts still need inspection and maintenance according to the product instructions.

items.question: Can gutters be installed when fascia is damaged?

children.text: Damaged fascia or other roof-edge support may need repair first. The estimate should identify that work or explain how concealed damage will be handled.

items.question: Does Roof King provide free gutter estimates?

children.text: Yes. Roof King provides free inspections and estimates. Call our team or use the online calendar to discuss your gutter project.

children.text: Gutters collect water from the roof and carry it to a discharge point away from the house. Sagging runs, blocked outlets and downspouts that empty beside the foundation can interrupt that route.

Roof King & Restoration installs and replaces residential gutters in Columbus and surrounding Central Ohio communities. We look at the entire route water takes—from the roof edge through the gutter and downspout to its discharge point—before recommending a new system. Call (614) 490-0123 to discuss a gutter estimate or book an inspection.

sections.title: When Should You Replace Your Gutters?

children.text: Not every drip means the whole system needs replacement. An isolated joint or outlet may be repairable when the surrounding gutter and support are still sound. But widespread sagging, recurring overflow, corrosion, loose attachment or repeated leaks at several locations can make replacement the more practical choice.

Pay attention to water staining on siding, peeling paint near the roof edge, washed-out landscaping and water pooling next to the house. These symptoms do not always begin at the gutter. A blocked downspout, poor discharge route or an adjoining roof-edge defect may be involved. We want to identify the cause before recommending work.

cards.title: Downspouts and Drainage Away From the House

children.text: The gutter is only the first part of the drainage route. Downspouts need to be located where they can receive the water collected from the roof, and the outlet needs a sensible discharge location. Water that empties next to a foundation or across a frequently used path can still create problems even when the gutter itself is in good condition.

Underground drain lines and site grading are separate systems. If those are blocked or poorly designed, new gutters alone may not solve the issue. The estimate should explain which discharge components Roof King will install and which conditions require a separate contractor or additional evaluation.

Residential Gutter Installation in Columbus

The roofline determines how the gutter system needs to collect water. The roof area, valleys, corners and pitch influence where runoff collects. The gutter profile, outlet positions and downspouts need to work together so water moves off the house instead of spilling behind the fascia or across a walkway.

We review the condition of the roof edge and discuss the layout of each gutter run. If fascia or adjacent trim is deteriorated, that needs to be addressed before a new gutter is fastened in place. The written proposal should identify the materials, attachment method, downspout locations and any preparation or removal work.

Seamless Gutter Runs and Connections

Seamless gutters are formed in long, continuous runs, reducing the number of joints along straight roof edges. Corners, end caps and outlets still require connections. The shape and length of the roofline determine how the system should be laid out.
See our dedicated seamless gutters page for the installation details.
When Should You Replace Your Gutters?

Not every drip means the whole system needs replacement. An isolated joint or outlet may be repairable when the surrounding gutter and support are still sound. A gutter is attached to a roof edge that also includes fascia, soffit, siding and roofing details. If those components are damaged, simply fastening a new gutter over them can leave the underlying problem unresolved.
Roof King also works on residential roofs and siding. When related exterior repairs are needed, we can discuss the sequence of work and identify what belongs in the gutter work.
For a roof-edge leak, review roof repair services.
For damaged wall cladding or trim, see siding services.
How do I know whether to repair or replace my gutters?

A localized joint, outlet or hanger issue may be repairable. Multiple failing sections, corrosion, widespread sagging or damaged supporting materials can make replacement more sensible. The condition of the existing system matters more than its age alone.
Are seamless gutters completely leak-free?
No. Seamless construction reduces joints along straight runs, but corners, end caps and outlets still require connections. Installation details and maintenance remain important.
Will larger gutters stop overflowing?
Not necessarily. Blocked outlets, poor slope, insufficient downspout capacity or discharge problems can still cause overflow. The whole drainage route needs to be evaluated.
Do gutter guards eliminate cleaning?
No. Guards can reduce certain debris entry, but the gutter, outlets and downspouts still need inspection and maintenance according to the product instructions.
Can gutters be installed when fascia is damaged?
Damaged fascia or other roof-edge support may need repair first. The estimate should identify that work or explain how concealed damage will be handled.
Does Roof King provide free gutter estimates?
Yes. Roof King provides free inspections and estimates. Call our team or use the online calendar to discuss your gutter project.

If your gutters overflow, pull away from the house or no longer direct water where it should go, tell us which areas are affected and what happens during heavy rain. Roof King can discuss an inspection and the next step toward a written estimate. Call (614) 490-0123 or book an appointment online.

Gutter guards can help reduce the amount of leaves and other debris entering a gutter. They do not correct an undersized outlet, poor gutter slope or damaged downspout, and they do not make maintenance unnecessary. The guard needs to suit the existing gutter, roof edge and the debris that collects there.

opening.title: How to Recognize an Ice Dam

children.text: Icicles by themselves do not prove that a roof has an ice dam. Look for a solid ridge of ice at the eaves with snow or meltwater sitting above it. Water stains, damp insulation and active leaks near outside walls are warning signs of water entry.
Uneven snow melt can be another clue. If snow disappears from the upper roof while a thick frozen band remains at the edge, heat escaping into the attic may be warming the roof deck.
Signs worth reporting when you contact Roof King:
Ice forming in a continuous band along the roof edge or in a valley.
Ceiling stains, damp drywall or dripping near an exterior wall.
Water behind the fascia, or gutters pulling away under the weight of ice.
Repeated ice buildup on the same roof section after snowstorms.

items.tabLabel: Why Snow Melts and Refreezes at the Eaves
items.title: Why Snow Melts and Refreezes at the Eaves

children.text: Snow on a warmer part of the roof melts and flows downhill. When that water reaches the colder eave, it freezes again. Repeated melting and freezing can build a thick ridge of ice along the roof edge.

Warm air leaking into an attic, insulation gaps and some roof or ventilation conditions can warm the upper roof while the eaves remain below freezing. Weather and sun exposure can also affect the pattern.

items.title: Right after the storm

children.text: Safety comes first. Then slow down any water coming in, and only then start recording what happened. None of it requires you to go on the roof.

items.description: Safety comes first. Then slow down any water coming in, and only then start recording what happened. None of it requires you to go on the roof.
items.label: Explore Storm Damage Documentation

cards.title: Stay off the roof and clear of hazards
cards.description: Damage you can see from the ground is enough to start with. Don't climb up or pull at loose material.

children.text: Stay out of rooms with sagging or soaked ceilings, and out of any building with visible structural damage until a professional clears it . If you smell gas, leave right away and call Columbia Gas from outside . Downed power lines are a 911 call . Don't use wet electrical equipment until a licensed electrician has checked it . Run a generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house .

cards.title: Slow the water down
cards.description: Temporary protection limits damage while the permanent repair is planned. It doesn't replace the repair.

children.text: Move belongings out of the way, catch drips and start drying wet materials within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold . If water is coming through the roof, call (614) 490-0123. Call Roof King to discuss temporary protection and inspection availability . Keep receipts for tarps, buckets, fans and any temporary repairs . Ask what the tarp covers and what permanent work is still needed.

cards.title: Photograph before you clean up
cards.description: Your own dated photos and video are the first part of the storm record.

children.text: Walk all four sides of the house and take wide shots from the ground, then close-ups of shingles in the yard, gutters, siding, screens and windows . Inside, photograph ceiling stains, wet insulation you can see from the attic hatch, and damaged belongings . Note the date and time of the storm and when you first noticed each problem. Don't throw out damaged items until your insurer says you can .

cards.title: Report the damage to your insurer yourself
cards.description: Policies can have reporting deadlines, so contact your insurer promptly and ask what records it needs .

children.text: Keep your policy number handy . Calling a roofer does not start a claim, and Roof King does not file one on your behalf . The
insurance claims tab
explains who does what.

cards.title: Find the storm date
cards.description: The storm report lists NOAA hail and wind reports near your address since 2019 .

children.text: These are reports, not a record of every hailstone. Hail falls in narrow bands, so a quiet result doesn't prove your roof is fine, and a nearby report doesn't prove it was hit . What the report gives you is a likely date.

image.alt: Supplied photograph of a shingle roof above a porch and adjoining exterior

items.caption: Residential exterior photograph supplied by Roof King; location is not asserted.

items.title: What damage to look for

children.text: Storm damage rarely stops at the shingles. Here is what to look for on each part of the house, and which parts only show up when someone inspects the roof itself.

items.description: Storm damage rarely stops at the shingles. Here is what to look for on each part of the house, and which parts only show up when someone inspects the roof itself.
items.label: Explore Storm Damage Documentation

groups.title: What damage to look for — Details

cards.title: Shingles
cards.description: Missing, lifted or creased shingles after wind; bruising, cracks or exposed mat after hail .

children.text: Shingle pieces in the yard and fresh granules at the downspouts are clues. Granules also wash off as a roof ages, so they aren't proof on their own. Hail bruises rarely show from the ground, which is why Roof King photographs every slope, not just the side facing the street .

cards.title: Edges, flashing and vents
cards.description: Roof edges, ridges and the flashing at walls, chimneys and pipes are where wind gets a grip.

children.text: Look for bent or lifted metal at the roof edge, flashing pulled away from a wall or chimney, and dented or cracked vent caps. Roof King inspects flashing, penetrations, valleys and transitions one by one .

cards.title: Attic and ceilings
cards.description: New stains, damp insulation or daylight through the roof boards mean water or debris got through.

children.text: Look only from the attic hatch with a flashlight, and don't step between joists. Roof King checks the attic where there's access, for moisture and ventilation .

cards.title: Gutters and downspouts
cards.description: Dents, pulled hangers and sagging runs are common after hail and wind.

children.text: A dented gutter tells you hail fell. It doesn't, by itself, mean the shingles need replacing . Gutter, fascia and other soft-metal damage gets recorded separately during the inspection . See
gutter services

cards.title: Siding and trim
cards.description: Look for cracked, punctured or missing panels and dented trim, usually worst on the side that faced the storm.

children.text: Siding and trim damage should get its own lines on the estimate, separate from the roof. See
siding services

cards.title: Windows and screens
cards.description: Torn screens, cracked glass and dented frames or wraps.

children.text: Watch for new drafts or leaks around a window in the days after a storm. See
window replacement

image.alt: Illustration of step flashing where shingles meet a brick chimney

items.caption: Illustration: roof-to-wall connections need their own assessment.

items.title: Hail vs wind damage

children.text: The National Weather Service treats a thunderstorm as severe when it brings winds of 58 mph or more, hail 1 inch across or larger, or both . Smaller storms can still damage a worn roof, and a severe storm doesn't guarantee damage. Hail and wind also leave different patterns.
NWS Severe Thunderstorm Criteria

items.description: The National Weather Service treats a thunderstorm as severe when it brings winds of 58 mph or more, hail 1 inch across or larger, or both . Smaller storms can still damage a worn roof, and a severe storm doesn't guarantee damage. Hail and wind also leave different patterns.
items.label: Explore Storm Damage Documentation

cards.title: Hail damage
cards.description: Impact marks scattered across a slope: bruises, cracks, missing granules and dents in soft metal.

children.text: Damage can vary slope by slope, so the inspection marks and documents test squares on each slope where hail is suspected . Vents, gutters and flashing are recorded on their own, because a dent in metal doesn't prove the shingles are damaged . More on the
hail damage roof repair
page .

cards.title: Wind damage
cards.description: Wind damage starts at edges, ridges and corners and shows up as missing, lifted or creased shingles.

children.text: A shingle can lift, crease and lose its seal without blowing off, so the courses around a missing piece need checking too. Displaced flashing can open a gap at a wall or chimney . More on the
wind damage roof repair
page , and in
why fall gusts over 40 mph matter

cards.title: Trees and large debris
cards.description: A falling limb can break roof boards, rafters and gutters, not just shingles.

children.text: Have the tree removed by a tree professional before any roof work, and stay out of rooms below until the structure is checked . One customer's tree-damage job ended with new roofs and gutters on two homes .

Applies to appropriately labeled packages. Impact testing does not guarantee protection from hail damage; confirm current product labeling.

items.title: Repair or replace after a storm

children.text: Storm damage doesn't automatically mean a new roof. The answer depends on how much of the roof is affected, the condition of the shingles that are left, and whether a repair can match and tie in.

items.description: Storm damage doesn't automatically mean a new roof. The answer depends on how much of the roof is affected, the condition of the shingles that are left, and whether a repair can match and tie in.

groups.title: Repair or replace after a storm — Details

cards.title: When a repair makes sense
cards.description: Damage is limited to one area, the rest of the roof is in good shape, and compatible shingles are available.

children.text: The repair usually covers more than the visible gap, so the new shingles can be woven in and sealed properly. See
roof repair in Columbus

cards.title: When replacement makes sense
cards.description: Damage on several slopes, shingles too brittle to take a repair, or leaks that keep coming back.

children.text: The recommendation should say which findings point to replacement. See
roof replacement
and
what a new roof costs

cards.title: Matching the old roof
cards.description: Weathering, color changes and discontinued lines can make a repair stand out.

children.text: Look at the proposed shingle next to your roof before you agree to a partial repair.

cards.title: When a new layer isn't allowed
cards.description: Ohio's residential code doesn't allow a new layer over some roofs.

children.text: Under Ohio Residential Code R908.3.1.1, a new roof can't go over an existing one that is water-soaked or deteriorated, that is slate, clay, cement or asbestos-cement tile, or that already has two or more layers . Storm-soaked roofs often fall into the first group.
Ohio Residential Roof Assembly Rules

cards.title: Columbus permits
cards.description: Inside Columbus city limits, replacing a roof requires a building permit, though not plan review .

children.text: Properties in historic or other special districts, such as German Village, may need extra approvals before work starts .

items.title: Insurance claims in Ohio

children.text: Your insurer decides what's covered. Roof King inspects, documents and explains the construction findings, and you deal with your insurer . Ohio law treats anyone who, for pay, acts for a homeowner in negotiating or settling a property claim as a public insurance adjuster, and a public adjuster needs a state certificate . Roof King doesn't negotiate your claim. Full detail is on
storm damage insurance claims

cards.title: You
cards.description: You report the claim, answer the insurer's questions and approve the work.

children.text: Share your photos, receipts and Roof King's findings with your insurer. Any further help from a contractor should be agreed in writing, not assumed .

cards.title: Your insurer
cards.description: The insurer inspects, applies your policy and decides coverage and payment .

children.text: No contractor's estimate or inspection can guarantee approval. If you have a coverage or claim dispute, the Ohio Department of Ins urance will take a complaint at no cost .
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Roof King
cards.description: Roof King inspects, photographs and gives you written findings and an estimate, whether or not there's a claim .

children.text: We explain what we found and what work we propose. We don't file claims on your behalf , and we don't negotiate or settle claims .
Ohio Public Adjuster Licensing Requirements

cards.title: Public adjusters
cards.description: A public adjuster works for you, for a fee, to negotiate the claim, and must be certified in Ohio .

children.text: If you're considering one, check their status with the Ohio Department of Insurance before you sign.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules
Ohio Public Adjuster Licensing Requirements

cards.title: Door-to-door offers
cards.description: Contractors often knock on doors after a storm. Take your time.

children.text: Check that the company is registered with the Ohio Secretary of State, and look it up with the BBB . Get more than one estimate and a written contract, and don't pay in full upfront . Under Ohio's home solicitation sales law, if you sign at your home you can usually cancel in writing before midnight of the third business day . Be wary of any offer to cover or waive your deductible .
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

items.question: Should I call my insurance company or a roofer first?

children.text: You can do both. Report the damage to your insurer promptly, because policies can have reporting deadlines . A Roof King inspection gives you written findings to share. Calling us does not start a claim .

items.question: What if I can't see any damage from the ground?

children.text: That's common with hail. Bruised shingles and lifted tabs rarely show from the yard. Tell us the storm date and any new leaks or stains, and stay off the roof. The inspection covers every slope .

items.question: Will Roof King deal with my insurance company for me?

children.text: No. In Ohio, negotiating or settling a property claim for a homeowner, for pay, is the work of a certified public insurance adjuster . Roof King provides the inspection photos, findings and estimate and explains them. You deal with your insurer .

items.question: Does storm damage mean I need a new roof?

children.text: Not necessarily. Isolated damage on a sound roof can often be repaired. Widespread damage, or shingles too worn to take a repair, points to replacement. The findings should show which applies.

items.question: Is the storm damage inspection free?

children.text: Yes. It's free with no obligation, and you keep the documented findings whether or not you hire Roof King .

items.question: Can you tarp my roof if it's leaking?

children.text: Call (614) 490-0123 and describe where the water is coming in. Ask about temporary protection and inspection availability . A tarp is temporary, and the estimate will list the permanent repair separately.

items.question: Do I need a permit for storm damage roof repair in Columbus?

children.text: Replacing a roof inside Columbus city limits requires a building permit, but not plan review, and historic districts may need extra approval . For a smaller repair, ask what your project needs. Get your storm damage inspected

quote.title: Get Your Storm Damage Inspected
quote.description: Send the property address, when you noticed the damage and a description of any active leak. Roof King can help you arrange the next step. For a business or managed building, use commercial storm restoration to review roof access, operations and building records.

Safety comes first. Then slow down any water coming in, and only then start recording what happened. None of it requires you to go on the roof.

Stay out of rooms with sagging or soaked ceilings, and out of any building with visible structural damage until a professional clears it . If you smell gas, leave right away and call Columbia Gas from outside . Downed power lines are a 911 call . Don't use wet electrical equipment until a licensed electrician has checked it . Run a generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house .

Move belongings out of the way, catch drips and start drying wet materials within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold . If water is coming through the roof, call (614) 490-0123. Call Roof King to discuss temporary protection and inspection availability . Keep receipts for tarps, buckets, fans and any temporary repairs . Ask what the tarp covers and what permanent work is still needed.

Walk all four sides of the house and take wide shots from the ground, then close-ups of shingles in the yard, gutters, siding, screens and windows . Inside, photograph ceiling stains, wet insulation you can see from the attic hatch, and damaged belongings . Note the date and time of the storm and when you first noticed each problem. Don't throw out damaged items until your insurer says you can .
Keep your policy number handy . Calling a roofer does not start a claim, and Roof King does not file one on your behalf . Theinsurance claims tab explains who does what.

These are reports, not a record of every hailstone. Hail falls in narrow bands, so a quiet result doesn't prove your roof is fine, and a nearby report doesn't prove it was hit . What the report gives you is a likely date.
Storm damage rarely stops at the shingles. Here is what to look for on each part of the house, and which parts only show up when someone inspects the roof itself.

Shingle pieces in the yard and fresh granules at the downspouts are clues. Granules also wash off as a roof ages, so they aren't proof on their own. Hail bruises rarely show from the ground, which is why Roof King photographs every slope, not just the side facing the street .

Look for bent or lifted metal at the roof edge, flashing pulled away from a wall or chimney, and dented or cracked vent caps. Roof King inspects flashing, penetrations, valleys and transitions one by one .
Look only from the attic hatch with a flashlight, and don't step between joists. Roof King checks the attic where there's access, for moisture and ventilation .

A dented gutter tells you hail fell. It doesn't, by itself, mean the shingles need replacing . Gutter, fascia and other soft-metal damage gets recorded separately during the inspection . Seegutter services .
Siding and trim damage should get its own lines on the estimate, separate from the roof. See siding services .
Watch for new drafts or leaks around a window in the days after a storm. Seewindow replacement .

The National Weather Service treats a thunderstorm as severe when it brings winds of 58 mph or more, hail 1 inch across or larger, or both . Smaller storms can still damage a worn roof, and a severe storm doesn't guarantee damage. Hail and wind also leave different patterns.
NWS Severe Thunderstorm Criteria

Damage can vary slope by slope, so the inspection marks and documents test squares on each slope where hail is suspected . Vents, gutters and flashing are recorded on their own, because a dent in metal doesn't prove the shingles are damaged . More on thehail damage roof repair page .

A shingle can lift, crease and lose its seal without blowing off, so the courses around a missing piece need checking too. Displaced flashing can open a gap at a wall or chimney . More on thewind damage roof repair page , and in why fall gusts over 40 mph matter .

Have the tree removed by a tree professional before any roof work, and stay out of rooms below until the structure is checked . One customer's tree-damage job ended with new roofs and gutters on two homes .

Storm damage doesn't automatically mean a new roof. The answer depends on how much of the roof is affected, the condition of the shingles that are left, and whether a repair can match and tie in.
The repair usually covers more than the visible gap, so the new shingles can be woven in and sealed properly. Seeroof repair in Columbus .
The recommendation should say which findings point to replacement. See roof replacement andwhat a new roof costs .
Look at the proposed shingle next to your roof before you agree to a partial repair.

Under Ohio Residential Code R908.3.1.1, a new roof can't go over an existing one that is water-soaked or deteriorated, that is slate, clay, cement or asbestos-cement tile, or that already has two or more layers . Storm-soaked roofs often fall into the first group.
Ohio Residential Roof Assembly Rules
Properties in historic or other special districts, such as German Village, may need extra approvals before work starts .

Your insurer decides what's covered. Roof King inspects, documents and explains the construction findings, and you deal with your insurer . Ohio law treats anyone who, for pay, acts for a homeowner in negotiating or settling a property claim as a public insurance adjuster, and a public adjuster needs a state certificate . Share your photos, receipts and Roof King's findings with your insurer. Any further help from a contractor should be agreed in writing, not assumed .

We explain what we found and what work we propose. We don't file claims on your behalf , and we don't negotiate or settle claims .

items.title: Signs of hail damage

children.text: Real hail damage is random. Hits land scattered across a slope in different sizes, and the same storm marks the metal, siding and screens around the roof. A neat row of marks, or damage on one spot only, usually points to something else. Look from the ground or a window. Checking the roof surface is our job.

items.description: Real hail damage is random. Hits land scattered across a slope in different sizes, and the same storm marks the metal, siding and screens around the roof. A neat row of marks, or damage on one spot only, usually points to something else. Look from the ground or a window. Checking the roof surface is our job.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: Bruised shingles
cards.description: A hailstone can crush the asphalt and fiberglass mat under the granules without breaking the surface.

children.text: How a bruise shows up A dark, roughly round spot, often with granules pressed in or missing It gives slightly under a fingertip, like a soft spot on fruit. A blister doesn't. Bruises sit at random across the slope, more of them on the side that faced the storm They may not leak right away. The weakened spot can shed granules and crack later, which is why bruises are photographed and counted, not ignored.

cards.title: Granule loss
cards.description: Granules shield the asphalt from sun. Hail knocks them off in patches.

children.text: What granule loss does and doesn't prove Bare black spots on the shingle face, and heavy granules at downspout outlets after a storm Every roof sheds some granules with age, and new roofs shed loose ones in the first months. Granules in the gutter alone don't prove hail damage. What matters is exposed asphalt at impact points, matched to the storm date

cards.title: Cracks and mat fractures
cards.description: A hard hit can split the shingle and the fiberglass mat inside it.

children.text: Why fractures matter most A fracture is a break through the shingle. It can let water reach the underlayment. Fractures are hard to see from the ground and often show only when the shingle is lifted or flexed by hand The impact test behind Class 4 ratings fails a shingle when a crack shows on the back after two hits in the same spot, which is why fractures are treated as functional damage

cards.title: Soft metals on the roof
cards.description: Box vents, ridge vents, pipe flashing, valley metal, chimney caps and skylight curbs dent easily.

children.text: What dents tell us Dents show that hail hit and roughly how big it was, and which direction it came from A dented vent can be cosmetic, but a split or crushed one can leak Metal damage is recorded on its own line. A dented vent doesn't by itself mean the shingles failed.

cards.title: Gutters, downspouts and fascia
cards.description: Gutters often show the clearest hail marks on the house.

children.text: Cosmetic or functional Dents along the front lip and the top of downspout elbows A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often cosmetic. Split seams, crushed sections or pulled hangers aren't. Gutter work is quoted separately and handled through our
gutter services

cards.title: Siding, window screens and sills
cards.description: Hail strong enough to damage a roof usually marks the walls, fences and cars nearby too.

children.text: Check the side that faced the storm Cracked or holed vinyl siding, chipped paint on wood or fiber cement, dented aluminum trim Torn or dented window screens and dented metal window wraps Spatter marks on decks, fences and outdoor equipment help date the storm Siding repairs go through our
siding services
; windows through
windows

cards.title: Damage that only looks like hail
cards.description: Several roof problems get mistaken for hail.

children.text: Look-alikes we rule out Blisters: raised or popped bubbles from trapped moisture or heat. No bruise underneath. Normal wear: even granule thinning across a whole slope, often worst on the south and west faces Foot traffic or tools: scuffs near walkways, ladders and the ridge Old repairs or manufacturing marks: patterns that repeat across the roof. Hail doesn't make patterns.

items.title: Hail size and your roof

children.text: Size isn't everything. Shingle type, age, wind and the angle of impact all change what a storm does. Still, size is the first thing an adjuster and a roofer ask about, so it helps to know the reference points.

cards.title: What forecasters call severe hail
cards.description: NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory considers hail quarter size, 1 inch across, or larger to be severe.

children.text: Size comparisons Quarter: 1 inch, the severe threshold Half dollar: roughly 1¼ inches Size means the diameter of the hailstone.

cards.title: When shingles start to show damage
cards.description: Damage depends on the shingle and its condition, not just the storm.

children.text: What one state regulator advises homeowners The Nebraska Department of Insurance says hail generally needs to be about 1¼ inches across before it damages a roof. Lightweight composite shingles can show damage from 1-inch hail, and only deteriorated shingles are usually damaged by hail under 1 inch. An older, brittle roof can be damaged by hail a newer roof shrugs off, which is why we look at the roof's age and condition alongside the storm.

cards.title: Wind-driven hail
cards.description: Hail falling at an angle hits one side of the house harder.

children.text: Why one slope can look worse Slopes, walls and screens facing the storm take more and harder hits. Slopes on the far side can be untouched. We record each slope separately for that reason.

cards.title: Finding the storm date
cards.description: Your insurer will ask when the damage happened.

children.text: Where storm reports come from NOAA's Storm Events Database records hail where someone reported it, such as a trained spotter, a law-enforcement officer or a member of the public. A report a mile away doesn't prove your roof was hit, and no nearby report doesn't prove it wasn't. Hail falls in narrow, uneven bands. Your own dated photos of hail on the ground, dented cars or spatter marks are often the best record.

cards.title: How UL 2218 works
cards.description: Steel balls are dropped onto shingles. Each class uses a bigger ball.

items.question: What size hail damages a roof?

children.text: NOAA's severe-storm lab treats hail 1 inch across (quarter size) or larger as severe. Whether it damages your roof depends on the shingles and their age. The Nebraska Department of Insurance says damage generally starts around 1¼ inches, lightweight shingles can be damaged by 1-inch hail, and older, deteriorated shingles by smaller stones. An inspection settles it for your roof.

items.question: Can a roof have hail damage without leaking?

children.text: Yes. Bruises and small fractures often don't leak at first. They weaken the shingle so it loses granules and cracks over time. That's why we record and count hits after a storm instead of waiting for a stain on the ceiling. See the "Signs of hail damage" tab above.

items.question: Will Roof King handle my insurance claim?

children.text: No. You file the claim and talk with your insurer, and your insurer decides coverage and payment. We inspect the roof, document the damage and explain our findings and estimate so you can share them. We speak with your insurer only if you ask us to and we agree on it first. In Ohio, negotiating a claim settlement for pay is reserved for licensed public insurance adjusters. More on
storm damage documentation

items.question: Does a hail inspection cost anything?

children.text: No. Our inspection is no cost and no obligation, and you get written findings with photos whether or not you hire us. It typically takes 45 to 90 minutes, depending on the size and complexity of the roof.

items.question: Do Class 4 shingles lower my insurance premium?

children.text: Some insurers offer a credit for impact-rated roofs and some don't, so ask your insurer what it offers and what proof it needs. We can give you the product name and the documents from your project. Class 4 means a shingle passed the UL 2218 test with a 2-inch steel ball. It doesn't make a roof hail-proof. See the Class 4 lines in the tab above.

items.question: Does a dented gutter mean my roof needs replacing?

children.text: Not by itself. Gutters and vents dent more easily than shingles, so dents show that hail hit, not that the shingles failed. We check the shingles on their own and list gutters separately. A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often a cosmetic repair.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace a hail-damaged roof in Columbus?

children.text: Yes, inside city limits. The City of Columbus requires a building permit, without plan review, to replace a roof. Historic and special zoning districts such as German Village may need extra approvals, and suburbs set their own rules.

items.question: What if the roof is leaking now?

children.text: Call

, tell us where water is showing and when the storm hit, and ask about current availability. Until then, catch the water, move belongings and stay off the roof. Keep receipts for anything you do to protect the house. Temporary protection and the permanent repair are separate steps. See

sections.title: How We Document a Hail Damage Inspection

children.text: A hail record should be understandable to you, your insurer or another roofer. Photograph each slope and material separately and note what could not be reached.

Where hail damage is suspected, the inspector marks a test square on each slope and records and photographs the observations. The front of the house and the back are assessed rather than assuming every slope has the same condition.

Dents in vents, flashing and skylight curbs are recorded as collateral observations. Any components needing repair are listed separately from the shingles; a dent alone does not establish that the roof covering failed.

Real hail damage is random. Hits land scattered across a slope in different sizes, and the same storm marks the metal, siding and screens around the roof. A neat row of marks, or damage on one spot only, usually points to something else. Look from the ground or a window. Checking the roof surface is our job.

How a bruise shows up A dark, roughly round spot, often with granules pressed in or missing It gives slightly under a fingertip, like a soft spot on fruit. A blister doesn't. Bruises sit at random across the slope, more of them on the side that faced the storm They may not leak right away. The weakened spot can shed granules and crack later, which is why bruises are photographed and counted, not ignored.

What granule loss does and doesn't prove Bare black spots on the shingle face, and heavy granules at downspout outlets after a storm Every roof sheds some granules with age, and new roofs shed loose ones in the first months. Granules in the gutter alone don't prove hail damage. What matters is exposed asphalt at impact points, matched to the storm date

Why fractures matter most A fracture is a break through the shingle. It can let water reach the underlayment. Fractures are hard to see from the ground and often show only when the shingle is lifted or flexed by hand The impact test behind Class 4 ratings fails a shingle when a crack shows on the back after two hits in the same spot, which is why fractures are treated as functional damage

What dents tell us Dents show that hail hit and roughly how big it was, and which direction it came from A dented vent can be cosmetic, but a split or crushed one can leak Metal damage is recorded on its own line. A dented vent doesn't by itself mean the shingles failed.

Cosmetic or functional Dents along the front lip and the top of downspout elbows A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often cosmetic. Split seams, crushed sections or pulled hangers aren't. Gutter work is quoted separately and handled through ourgutter services

Look-alikes we rule out Blisters: raised or popped bubbles from trapped moisture or heat. No bruise underneath. Normal wear: even granule thinning across a whole slope, often worst on the south and west faces Foot traffic or tools: scuffs near walkways, ladders and the ridge Old repairs or manufacturing marks: patterns that repeat across the roof. Hail doesn't make patterns.

Why one slope can look worse Slopes, walls and screens facing the storm take more and harder hits. Slopes on the far side can be untouched. We record each slope separately for that reason.

A report a mile away doesn't prove your roof was hit, and no nearby report doesn't prove it wasn't. Hail falls in narrow, uneven bands. Signs a repair is enough A handful of bruised or fractured shingles on one or two slopes Dented vents or flashing that can be swapped without disturbing much roofing Surrounding shingles that are still flexible and hold their granules A shingle line that's still made in a close color Seeroof repair .

Signs a repair stops making sense Bruises or fractures on most slopes Widespread granule loss at impact points A brittle, older roof that cracks when shingles are lifted for a repair A discontinued line that can't be matched on a visible slope

What to expect Weathering changes color, and lines get discontinued. We show you the closest available match before work starts, and we're honest when a patch would stand out. Whether insurance pays for matching is a policy question for your insurer.

What the city says "Replace roof" requires a permit but not plan review, according to the city's Typical Residential Projects guide. Homes in special zoning or historic districts, such as German Village, may need additional approvals. Suburbs and townships outside Columbus city limits set their own rules.
A hail record should be understandable to you, your insurer or another roofer. Photograph each slope and material separately and note what could not be reached.

Where hail damage is suspected, the inspector marks a test square on each slope and records and photographs the observations. The front of the house and the back are assessed rather than assuming every slope has the same condition.

Dents in vents, flashing and skylight curbs are recorded as collateral observations. Any components needing repair are listed separately from the shingles; a dent alone does not establish that the roof covering failed.

Gutters, siding and screens receive separate photographs and estimate lines. Where the attic is accessible, the underside of the deck is checked for water. The findings distinguish the observed condition of each component.
A written estimate should identify the actual work and allow a line-by-line comparison:

Observed damage by slope, with photos and test-square observations.Shingles, underlayment, flashing, vents and ridge components being replaced.The connection to retained roofing and expected color match.Separate gutter, fascia, siding and interior work.Removal, preparation, cleanup and written coverage.

If removal reveals damaged decking or another concealed condition, the additional work should be documented, priced and approved before proceeding. Construction findings are not an insurer’s agreement to pay.

Identify the shingle line, profile, finish and related flashings. Discuss aging, discontinued products and how close a replacement can match the retained roof. Include the adjoining repairs needed to restore the affected connection.

Review the written contract before work begins, including payment stages and the completion record. For covered Ohio home-solicitation sales, the cancellation period generally runs until midnight of the third business day after signing; the applicable agreement and statutory rules govern.
Ohio Home-Solicitation Cancellation Rules

Tell us the storm date, the address and anything you’ve noticed, such as dented gutters, granules at the downspouts or a new stain. You’ll get photos and a written recommendation to share with your insurer if you choose.

NOAA's severe-storm lab treats hail 1 inch across (quarter size) or larger as severe. Whether it damages your roof depends on the shingles and their age. The Nebraska Department of Insurance says damage generally starts around 1¼ inches, lightweight shingles can be damaged by 1-inch hail, and older, deteriorated shingles by smaller stones. An inspection settles it for your roof.

Yes. Bruises and small fractures often don't leak at first. They weaken the shingle so it loses granules and cracks over time. That's why we record and count hits after a storm instead of waiting for a stain on the ceiling. See the "Signs of hail damage" tab above.

No. You file the claim and talk with your insurer, and your insurer decides coverage and payment. We inspect the roof, document the damage and explain our findings and estimate so you can share them. We speak with your insurer only if you ask us to and we agree on it first. In Ohio, negotiating a claim settlement for pay is reserved for licensed public insurance adjusters. More onstorm damage documentation .

No. Our inspection is no cost and no obligation, and you get written findings with photos whether or not you hire us. It typically takes 45 to 90 minutes, depending on the size and complexity of the roof.

Some insurers offer a credit for impact-rated roofs and some don't, so ask your insurer what it offers and what proof it needs. We can give you the product name and the documents from your project. Class 4 means a shingle passed the UL 2218 test with a 2-inch steel ball. It doesn't make a roof hail-proof. See the Class 4 lines in the tab above.

Not by itself. Gutters and vents dent more easily than shingles, so dents show that hail hit, not that the shingles failed. We check the shingles on their own and list gutters separately. A gutter that still holds its slope and drains is often a cosmetic repair.

Yes, inside city limits. The City of Columbus requires a building permit, without plan review, to replace a roof. Historic and special zoning districts such as German Village may need extra approvals, and suburbs set their own rules.

Call(614) 490-0123, tell us where water is showing and when the storm hit, and ask about current availability. Until then, catch the water, move belongings and stay off the roof. Keep receipts for anything you do to protect the house. Temporary protection and the permanent repair are separate steps. Seestorm damage repairs .

items.title: Right after the storm

children.text: Severe straight-line wind happens here. On August 11, 2026, the National Weather Service measured an 82 mph gust at John Glenn Columbus International Airport and 70 mph at the Ohio State University Airport, and it attributed widespread Franklin County damage to straight-line winds of 60–80 mph . After a storm like that, the order matters: stay safe, limit water getting in, record the damage, then have the roof inspected.
NWS Franklin County Storm Survey — August 11, 2026

items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: Stay safe and stay off the roof
cards.description: Wind-damaged roofs are slick, loose and sometimes carrying limbs or wires.

children.text: Before anything else Contact emergency services for downed power lines, a structural collapse or fire. If you smell gas, leave the house and contact your gas utility from outside. Stay out of rooms or buildings with visible structural damage until a professional has checked them. Look and photograph from the ground or from inside. Don't climb up or pull at loose shingles, flashing or limbs.

cards.title: Slow the water down
cards.description: Temporary protection buys time. It isn't the repair.

children.text: What temporary protection does and doesn't do Inside: move belongings, catch drips and start drying wet materials. The City of Columbus advises starting within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold. On the roof: a temporary cover over an opening is installed where it's appropriate and available. Call (614) 490-0123 and describe the problem so availability can be discussed. Keep receipts for emergency supplies, temporary repairs and professional services. Temporary protection doesn't seal broken shingle bonds or reattach flashing. The estimate should say what it covers and what permanent work remains.

cards.title: Record it before cleanup
cards.description: Photos taken the day of the storm are the best record you'll have.

children.text: What to record Photos and video of every damaged area inside and out, with the date and time Shingles, ridge pieces, flashing or gutter sections in the yard. Photograph them where they landed and keep them. Ceiling stains, drips and attic wetness Don't throw away damaged items until your insurance carrier says it's acceptable. Our
storm documentation page
explains how inspection photos, the estimate and completed-work records fit together.

items.title: Shingles and seal strips

children.text: Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.

items.description: Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: Broken seal strips
cards.description: A shingle can look flat and still be unsealed.

children.text: Why the bond matters IBHS notes that wind can lift unsealed shingles and let water seep underneath. New shingles can take one to two months or more to seal in poor conditions. We check courses by hand on the windward slopes, where wind usually breaks the most bonds. A shingle that lifts freely along a whole course points to a wider bond failure, not a single loose piece.

cards.title: Creased shingles
cards.description: When wind lifts a shingle and drops it, the mat can fold across the nail line.

children.text: Why a crease counts as damage A crease is a break in the shingle's mat. It won't lie flat again or reseal reliably. Creases usually run in a line across several shingles on the same course. Creased shingles are replaced. Gluing them down leaves the fold in place.

cards.title: Missing shingles and exposed nails
cards.description: A blown-off shingle leaves nail heads and the course above it exposed.

children.text: What sits under the gap Exposed nails and nail holes let water track down into the underlayment and deck. We check whether the shingles around the gap were nailed correctly, because nail position affects how a shingle holds in wind. Underlayment and decking under the opening are checked before new shingles go on.

cards.title: Granules and scuffs
cards.description: Bare spots and fresh scuffs show where shingles flapped or debris dragged.

children.text: How we read them A heavy pile of granules at the downspouts after a storm is worth mentioning when you call. Scuffs alone may be cosmetic. Scuffs with lifted or creased shingles usually aren't. Hail leaves a different pattern. See
hail damage roof repair
if the storm brought both.

items.title: Ridges, edges, flashing and gutters

children.text: Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

items.description: Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

groups.title: Ridges, edges, flashing and gutters — Details

cards.title: Ridge and hip caps
cards.description: Ridge caps sit on the most exposed line of the roof.

children.text: What fails and how it's fixed Caps crack or blow off, exposing the ridge vent or the shingle tops underneath. Hip and ridge caps are made to bend over the seam and are fastened on each side above the sealant strip. A lost run of caps is replaced with a compatible cap product, and the ridge vent is checked for wind damage.

cards.title: Eaves and rakes
cards.description: Wind gets under the first course at the eaves and along the gable rakes.

children.text: Why the edge needs attention IBHS says the starter strip helps prevent water intrusion and protects against wind uplift at the roof edges. We check the starter course, the drip edge and the first shingle course for lifting. An edge that was never properly started tends to fail again. The estimate should say how the new edge will be built.

cards.title: Flashing
cards.description: Wind loosens step flashing, counterflashing and chimney flashing, opening a path for water.

children.text: What we check Step flashing along walls and dormers, chimney flashing and counterflashing, skylight and vent flanges Bent, lifted or face-caulked pieces are reset or replaced, not coated over The repair names the failed part rather than treating everything as a shingle replacement

cards.title: Gutters and downspouts
cards.description: Wind and falling limbs pull gutters away from the fascia and bend downspouts.

children.text: Gutters belong in the same inspection Gutters pulled from the fascia can let water behind them onto the fascia board and the roof edge. We note gutter and fascia damage separately on the estimate, not folded into the roof patch. Gutter repair and replacement are covered on our
gutter services page

items.title: Fallen trees and limbs

children.text: A tree or a large limb on the roof is a structural problem first and a roofing problem second. The roof can only be repaired properly once the tree is off and the framing and decking below have been checked.

items.description: A tree or a large limb on the roof is a structural problem first and a roofing problem second. The roof can only be repaired properly once the tree is off and the framing and decking below have been checked.

cards.title: Before the tree comes off
cards.description: Leave the tree where it is until it can be removed safely.

children.text: Safety first If lines are down or the structure is damaged, contact emergency services and stay clear. Photograph the tree on the roof from the ground and the damage from inside before anything is moved. A tree blocking the street can be reported to the City of Columbus. Damage entirely on private property is the owner's and their insurer's responsibility.

cards.title: What we check after removal
cards.description: An impact can crack rafters and decking well beyond the hole.

children.text: What the inspection covers Broken or cracked decking and any damaged rafters or trusses under the impact area Shingles, ridge, flashing and gutters along the path the tree took Siding, fascia and soffit damage where the tree hit the wall line Damaged wood is noted for repair before new roofing goes on

items.title: Wind ratings and shingles

children.text: Shingle packages list wind classifications from two different ASTM tests, plus a separate manufacturer wind warranty. They answer three different questions, and none of them means a roof can't be damaged by wind.

items.description: Shingle packages list wind classifications from two different ASTM tests, plus a separate manufacturer wind warranty. They answer three different questions, and none of them means a roof can't be damaged by wind.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: ASTM D3161 (Class A, D, F)
cards.description: A fan-driven test of shingles on a test deck.

children.text: What the class means IBHS describes D3161 as measuring a shingle's ability to withstand fan-induced wind speeds. Class F is the highest D3161 class. GAF lists it as 110 mph. The speed describes air flowing over the shingles in the lab, not the wind load on your house.

cards.title: ASTM D7158 (Class D, G, H)
cards.description: An uplift test that measures how strongly the sealed shingle resists being pulled up.

children.text: What the class means IBHS: D7158 assigns a class based on a two-part uplift test, and the classes tie to ASCE 7 wind zones. Class H is the highest D7158 class. GAF lists it as 150 mph. Both tests evaluate new product. IBHS notes they don't account for weathering or aging. An older roof doesn't keep its rating.

cards.title: Wind warranty is a separate promise
cards.description: A limited wind warranty is the manufacturer's coverage terms, not a test result.

children.text: What usually decides coverage The stated mph applies to a particular product, installed a particular way. Higher wind coverage often requires the manufacturer's starter, ridge and other accessories, extra nails or a special application. The product cards below show each line's conditions. Shingles generally need to have sealed. Damage from falling trees or debris is a different matter from blow-off. Your proposal names the product, and the manufacturer's warranty document sets the terms.

cards.description: In Ohio, settling a property claim on a homeowner's behalf is licensed work.

children.text: What Ohio law says Ohio defines a public insurance adjuster as anyone who, for compensation, acts on behalf of an insured in settling a property loss claim. That work requires a certificate of authority from the state. We stick to the roof. If you want someone to represent you on the claim, that's a licensed public adjuster or an attorney.

cards.description: For applicable replacement-cost settlements under Ohio’s rule, matching should produce a reasonably comparable appearance. How the rule applies depends on the covered loss and policy.

children.text: The Ohio matching rule When a replacement-cost policy pays to replace an item and the replacement doesn't match in quality, color or size, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace as much of the item as needed for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's decision under your policy. We document the product on your roof and what's currently available.

children.text: The City's checklist Confirm the contractor is registered with the Ohio Secretary of State. Get more than one estimate and a written contract before work starts. Don't pay in full upfront. Report suspected contractor fraud to the Ohio Attorney General through the agency's official website. Residential roofing in Columbus falls under the City's Home Improvement limited contractor license, which you can look up on the Citizen Access Portal.

items.question: How strong does wind have to be to damage a roof?

children.text: There's no single number. Shingle age, how well the courses sealed, nailing, roof shape and exposure all matter. Wind ratings are measured on new shingles in a lab, and IBHS notes the tests don't account for weathering or aging. Older roofs, edges and ridges usually fail first. After any storm that sends shingles into the yard, have the roof checked.

items.question: Can a few blown-off shingles be repaired, or does the whole roof need replacing?

children.text: Most wind damage is repairable. A repair makes sense when the damage is confined to identifiable areas and the surrounding shingles still seal and bend without cracking. Replacement belongs in the conversation when seal strips have failed across whole slopes or the old shingles are too brittle to work. You'll get the reason in writing either way. See
roof repair
for repairs beyond storm damage.

items.question: Will new shingles match the rest of my roof?

children.text: Often closely, but rarely perfectly. Weathering, color batches and discontinued lines all affect the match. We identify your shingle, show you the closest current product and tell you how it will look before work starts. For insured losses on a replacement-cost policy, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace enough for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's call.

items.question: Does homeowners insurance cover wind damage to a roof?

children.text: That depends on your policy and is decided by your insurer, not by Roof King. Contact your carrier promptly, because policies have reporting deadlines. We can inspect, photograph and document the damage and give you a written estimate for the work. The
storm documentation page
explains what those records contain.

items.question: Will Roof King negotiate my claim or act as my adjuster?

children.text: No. In Ohio, acting for a homeowner in settling a property claim for compensation is public insurance adjusting, which requires a state certificate of authority. We explain our construction findings and the proposed work. You may share our written construction findings with your insurer; coverage and payment remain between you and the insurer.

items.question: A tree fell on my roof. What should I do first?

children.text: Get everyone clear. Contact emergency services if power lines are down or the structure looks unsafe, and stay out of damaged rooms. Photograph the tree and the damage from the ground and from inside before anything is moved, and contact your insurer. Once the tree is off, the roof inspection should check the decking and framing under the impact, not just the shingles.

items.question: Do I need a permit for wind damage roof work in Columbus?

children.text: Inside City of Columbus limits, replacing a roof requires a building permit, with no plan review. Properties in special zoning or historic districts may need extra approvals. Ask whether your repair needs a permit and who will pull it. Suburbs outside the city set their own rules.

items.question: What do wind ratings and wind warranties on new shingles mean?

children.text: ASTM D3161 (up to Class F) and ASTM D7158 (up to Class H) are two different lab tests of new shingles. A limited wind warranty is the manufacturer's coverage, and higher speeds often depend on qualifying accessories and installation. For example, GAF's WindProven coverage requires a qualifying system. Neither makes a roof wind-proof. The Wind ratings tab above compares four lines we show on our site.

Roof King & Restoration provides wind damage roof repair for Columbus homes. We inspect the affected slope, not only the visible gap, photograph what we find and give you a written estimate that names each repair.
Water coming in now? Call (614) 490-0123, describe the active problem and ask about current availability.
