Choose what you’re dealing with. Each tab covers what wind does to that part of the roof, what we check and what a proper repair involves.

Severe straight-line wind happens here. On August 11, 2026, the National Weather Service measured an 82 mph gust at John Glenn Columbus International Airport and 70 mph at the Ohio State University Airport, and it attributed widespread Franklin County damage to straight-line winds of 60–80 mph . After a storm like that, the order matters: stay safe, limit water getting in, record the damage, then have the roof inspected.
NWS Franklin County Storm Survey — August 11, 2026

Before anything else Contact emergency services for downed power lines, a structural collapse or fire. If you smell gas, leave the house and contact your gas utility from outside. Stay out of rooms or buildings with visible structural damage until a professional has checked them. Look and photograph from the ground or from inside. Don't climb up or pull at loose shingles, flashing or limbs.

What temporary protection does and doesn't do Inside: move belongings, catch drips and start drying wet materials. The City of Columbus advises starting within 24 to 48 hours to limit mold. On the roof: a temporary cover over an opening is installed where it's appropriate and available. Call (614) 490-0123 and describe the problem so availability can be discussed. Keep receipts for emergency supplies, temporary repairs and professional services. Temporary protection doesn't seal broken shingle bonds or reattach flashing. The estimate should say what it covers and what permanent work remains.

What to record Photos and video of every damaged area inside and out, with the date and time Shingles, ridge pieces, flashing or gutter sections in the yard. Photograph them where they landed and keep them. Ceiling stains, drips and attic wetness Don't throw away damaged items until your insurance carrier says it's acceptable. Ourstorm documentation page explains how inspection photos, the estimate and completed-work records fit together.

Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.

Why the bond matters IBHS notes that wind can lift unsealed shingles and let water seep underneath. New shingles can take one to two months or more to seal in poor conditions. We check courses by hand on the windward slopes, where wind usually breaks the most bonds. A shingle that lifts freely along a whole course points to a wider bond failure, not a single loose piece.

Why a crease counts as damage A crease is a break in the shingle's mat. It won't lie flat again or reseal reliably. Creases usually run in a line across several shingles on the same course. Creased shingles are replaced. Gluing them down leaves the fold in place.

What sits under the gap Exposed nails and nail holes let water track down into the underlayment and deck. We check whether the shingles around the gap were nailed correctly, because nail position affects how a shingle holds in wind. Underlayment and decking under the opening are checked before new shingles go on.

How we read them A heavy pile of granules at the downspouts after a storm is worth mentioning when you call. Scuffs alone may be cosmetic. Scuffs with lifted or creased shingles usually aren't. Hail leaves a different pattern. Seehail damage roof repair if the storm brought both.
Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

What fails and how it's fixed Caps crack or blow off, exposing the ridge vent or the shingle tops underneath. Hip and ridge caps are made to bend over the seam and are fastened on each side above the sealant strip. A lost run of caps is replaced with a compatible cap product, and the ridge vent is checked for wind damage.

Why the edge needs attention IBHS says the starter strip helps prevent water intrusion and protects against wind uplift at the roof edges. We check the starter course, the drip edge and the first shingle course for lifting. An edge that was never properly started tends to fail again. The estimate should say how the new edge will be built.

What we check Step flashing along walls and dormers, chimney flashing and counterflashing, skylight and vent flanges Bent, lifted or face-caulked pieces are reset or replaced, not coated over The repair names the failed part rather than treating everything as a shingle replacement

Gutters belong in the same inspection Gutters pulled from the fascia can let water behind them onto the fascia board and the roof edge. We note gutter and fascia damage separately on the estimate, not folded into the roof patch. Gutter repair and replacement are covered on ourgutter services page .

A tree or a large limb on the roof is a structural problem first and a roofing problem second. The roof can only be repaired properly once the tree is off and the framing and decking below have been checked.

Safety first If lines are down or the structure is damaged, contact emergency services and stay clear. Photograph the tree on the roof from the ground and the damage from inside before anything is moved. A tree blocking the street can be reported to the City of Columbus. Damage entirely on private property is the owner's and their insurer's responsibility.

What the inspection covers Broken or cracked decking and any damaged rafters or trusses under the impact area Shingles, ridge, flashing and gutters along the path the tree took Siding, fascia and soffit damage where the tree hit the wall line Damaged wood is noted for repair before new roofing goes on

Shingle packages list wind classifications from two different ASTM tests, plus a separate manufacturer wind warranty. They answer three different questions, and none of them means a roof can't be damaged by wind.

What the class means IBHS describes D3161 as measuring a shingle's ability to withstand fan-induced wind speeds. Class F is the highest D3161 class. GAF lists it as 110 mph. The speed describes air flowing over the shingles in the lab, not the wind load on your house.

What the class means IBHS: D7158 assigns a class based on a two-part uplift test, and the classes tie to ASCE 7 wind zones. Class H is the highest D7158 class. GAF lists it as 150 mph. Both tests evaluate new product. IBHS notes they don't account for weathering or aging. An older roof doesn't keep its rating.

What usually decides coverage The stated mph applies to a particular product, installed a particular way. Higher wind coverage often requires the manufacturer's starter, ridge and other accessories, extra nails or a special application. The product cards below show each line's conditions. Shingles generally need to have sealed. Damage from falling trees or debris is a different matter from blow-off. Your proposal names the product, and the manufacturer's warranty document sets the terms.

Manufacturer-stated classification speeds under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual roof performance depends on roof design, exposure and installation; this is not a guaranteed storm speed or wind warranty.
Applies to appropriately labeled packages. Impact testing does not guarantee protection from hail damage; confirm current product labeling.
A laboratory classification is different from a wind warranty or a guaranteed storm speed.
Applies to the labeled product; impact testing does not promise a hail-proof roof.
Manufacturer laboratory classifications; not guaranteed storm speeds.
Product labeling and listed test standard govern the classification. Hail damage is not promised to be covered.

Wind is a common reason homeowners file a property claim. Your insurer decides whether the damage is covered and what it pays. Roof King's job is the roof: we inspect it, document what wind did, explain our findings and give you a written estimate for the work.

What the City of Columbus advises Contact your insurance carrier right away if you believe the property was damaged. Policies have deadlines for reporting claims. For help understanding a policy or disputing a decision, the Ohio Department of Insurance is at insurance.ohio.gov or insurance.ohio.gov. A roofing estimate doesn't decide whether a claim is approved or what it pays.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

Our part Inspection photos tied to locations on the roof, and written findings A written estimate that names the materials, the repairs and any adjoining work Completed-work records once the job is done You may share our construction findings and estimate with your insurer. Coverage and payment discussions remain between you and your insurer.

What Ohio law says Ohio defines a public insurance adjuster as anyone who, for compensation, acts on behalf of an insured in settling a property loss claim. That work requires a certificate of authority from the state. We stick to the roof. If you want someone to represent you on the claim, that's a licensed public adjuster or an attorney.
Ohio Public Adjuster Licensing Requirements

The Ohio matching rule When a replacement-cost policy pays to replace an item and the replacement doesn't match in quality, color or size, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace as much of the item as needed for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's decision under your policy. We document the product on your roof and what's currently available.

The City's checklist Confirm the contractor is registered with the Ohio Secretary of State. Get more than one estimate and a written contract before work starts. Don't pay in full upfront. Report suspected contractor fraud to the Ohio Attorney General through the agency's official website. Residential roofing in Columbus falls under the City's Home Improvement limited contractor license, which you can look up on the Citizen Access Portal.
Most wind damage is repairable. Wind alone doesn't make a roof a replacement case, and you should expect a clear reason before anyone recommends one.

Signs a repair will hold Missing or creased shingles on a few courses, a run of ridge caps or one flashing detail Shingles next to the damage still lie flat, seal and bend without cracking A compatible product is available, and you've seen how the color will compare

Signs a repair won't last Seal strips broken across whole slopes, not just a few courses Old shingles crack when lifted to weave in new ones Repeated blow-offs, or decking damage across a large area Ourroof replacement page covers materials, decking and what a full estimate includes.
What to ask Ask whether your project needs a permit and who will pull it. Properties in special zoning or historic districts may need extra approvals. Suburbs outside city limits set their own rules.

As our offers pages describe them System Plus: qualifying GAF shingles, at least three qualifying accessories and an eligible GAF-certified contractor. It extends initial non-prorated coverage for eligible products. Silver Pledge: four qualifying accessories and a Certified Plus or Master Elite contractor. It adds coverage for installation errors, for a period that depends on the shingle. Golden Pledge: five qualifying accessories, Master Elite contractors only, with installation-error coverage. These apply to new qualifying GAF roof systems, not to spot repairs. SeeGAF System Plus for the full terms.

Tell us when the wind came through, what you’ve found in the yard or on the ceiling, and whether water is getting in now. We’ll inspect the roof, document the findings and give you a written estimate for the repair.

There's no single number. Shingle age, how well the courses sealed, nailing, roof shape and exposure all matter. Wind ratings are measured on new shingles in a lab, and IBHS notes the tests don't account for weathering or aging. Older roofs, edges and ridges usually fail first. After any storm that sends shingles into the yard, have the roof checked.

Most wind damage is repairable. A repair makes sense when the damage is confined to identifiable areas and the surrounding shingles still seal and bend without cracking. Replacement belongs in the conversation when seal strips have failed across whole slopes or the old shingles are too brittle to work. You'll get the reason in writing either way. Seeroof repair for repairs beyond storm damage.

Often closely, but rarely perfectly. Weathering, color batches and discontinued lines all affect the match. We identify your shingle, show you the closest current product and tell you how it will look before work starts. For insured losses on a replacement-cost policy, Ohio's claims rule requires the insurer to replace enough for a reasonably comparable appearance. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's call.

That depends on your policy and is decided by your insurer, not by Roof King. Contact your carrier promptly, because policies have reporting deadlines. We can inspect, photograph and document the damage and give you a written estimate for the work. Thestorm documentation page explains what those records contain.

No. In Ohio, acting for a homeowner in settling a property claim for compensation is public insurance adjusting, which requires a state certificate of authority. We explain our construction findings and the proposed work. You may share our written construction findings with your insurer; coverage and payment remain between you and the insurer.

Get everyone clear. Contact emergency services if power lines are down or the structure looks unsafe, and stay out of damaged rooms. Photograph the tree and the damage from the ground and from inside before anything is moved, and contact your insurer. Once the tree is off, the roof inspection should check the decking and framing under the impact, not just the shingles.

Inside City of Columbus limits, replacing a roof requires a building permit, with no plan review. Properties in special zoning or historic districts may need extra approvals. Ask whether your repair needs a permit and who will pull it. Suburbs outside the city set their own rules.

ASTM D3161 (up to Class F) and ASTM D7158 (up to Class H) are two different lab tests of new shingles. A limited wind warranty is the manufacturer's coverage, and higher speeds often depend on qualifying accessories and installation. For example, GAF's WindProven coverage requires a qualifying system. Neither makes a roof wind-proof. The Wind ratings tab above compares four lines we show on our site.

cards.title: Read the declarations page

children.text: The deductible: a flat amount or a percentage. Some policies carry a separate deductible for wind or hail, or for the roof itself. Whether the roof is paid at replacement cost or actual cash value (see the deductibles tab). Any roof endorsement or exclusion. Your agent can explain wording you're unsure about.

cards.title: Note the deadlines in your policy
cards.description: Your policy sets how soon to report a loss and how long you have to finish repairs and claim any withheld money.

children.text: Reporting a loss: the policy says how promptly. Contact your carrier as soon as you suspect damage. Finishing repairs: replacement-cost policies often hold back part of the payment until the work is done; the policy sets the time limit. Insurer deadlines also apply in Ohio. The insurer must acknowledge your claim within 15 days and accept or deny it within 21 days of receiving a properly executed proof of loss, or tell you why it needs more time.

groups.title: Deductibles, depreciation and what the insurer pays — Details

cards.title: Your deductible
cards.description: The deductible is the part of a covered loss you pay. Some policies set a separate wind, hail or roof deductible.

children.text: Be cautious with any offer to cover or waive your insurance deductible. The reason: the insurer pays from the price it's told. In Ohio, knowingly presenting a false or misleading statement to an insurer to defraud it is insurance fraud. If paying the deductible is the problem, see financing below.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Actual cash value (ACV)
cards.description: ACV pays the roof's replacement cost minus depreciation for age and wear.

children.text: Ohio's claims rule: the insurer determines actual cash value from the replacement cost at the time of loss, including sales tax, less depreciation, and must give you documentation of the depreciation on request. NAIC's illustration: $15,000 of roof damage with $10,000 of depreciation and a $1,000 deductible pays $4,000 under ACV, against $14,000 under replacement cost. figures, not a Roof King price.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Replacement cost value (RCV)
cards.description: RCV pays to repair or replace the roof without subtracting depreciation, less your deductible.

children.text: Insurers often pay the actual cash value first and reimburse the withheld amount, called recoverable depreciation, after the work is done and the invoice is submitted. That's how North Carolina's insurance regulator describes it; check your own policy for the process and the deadline.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Matching new shingles to the old
cards.description: For applicable replacement-cost settlements under Ohio’s rule, matching should produce a reasonably comparable appearance. How the rule applies depends on the covered loss and policy.

items.question: Should I call my insurer or a roofer first?

items.question: What's the difference between ACV and replacement cost on a roof claim?

children.text: Actual cash value is the replacement cost minus depreciation; Ohio's rule lets you ask for documentation of every depreciation deduction. Replacement cost pays without subtracting depreciation, less your deductible, though insurers often hold part back until the work is finished.

items.question: How long does an Ohio insurer have to respond to my claim?

children.text: A roof insurance claim and the roof repair rest on the same facts: what the storm damaged, where and when. Roof King & Restoration inspects the roof, siding and gutters, documents the damage clearly and explains the insurance process so you can decide whether a claim makes sense. You file the claim and speak with your insurer, and your insurer decides coverage and payment.
Water coming in now? Call (614) 490-0123, describe the active problem and ask about current availability.

sections.title: Who Does What in an Ohio Roof Claim

children.text: Clear responsibilities help keep construction findings separate from policy decisions.

You report the claim, speak with your insurer and authorize the repair. Keep the policy, photos, correspondence and written proposals together. Avoid blank or incomplete contracts and record payments.

Your insurer investigates, decides coverage under the policy and handles payment. Ohio generally requires acknowledgement within 15 calendar days and an accept-or-deny decision within 21 days of properly executed proof of loss. If additional investigation is needed, the insurer must explain within that period and provide written status updates at least every 45 days.
Ohio’s Claim Acknowledgement and Investigation Rules

We inspect, document the observed condition, explain the construction findings and build the work you authorize. We do not negotiate or settle insurance claims. Paid public adjusting requires the applicable Ohio authority.

Roof replacement deserves consideration when the damage is widespread or the surrounding roof cannot support a satisfactory repair. The recommendation should explain which findings lead to that conclusion. Storm timing alone does not establish the cause or extent of every existing roof problem.
Your Dublin storm repair estimate and insurance documentation

Photographs, observations, the repair estimate and any later work changes can help explain the construction work. Coverage questions belong with your insurer and policy documents. A contractor's estimate does not itself establish a covered loss or guarantee payment. The storm documentation page explains the records to keep before and after repairs.

Keep the construction estimate and any later approved changes with the dated observations and photographs. Your insurer determines policy coverage; the roofing proposal explains the work and does not guarantee a claim outcome.

Send the property address, when you noticed the damage and a description of any active leak. Roof King can help you arrange the next step. For related services, visit roofing and exterior services in Dublin.
What if I cannot see damage from the ground?
Ground observations cannot establish every roof condition. Describe the storm, any new symptoms and previous repairs when requesting an assessment. Avoid climbing onto the roof to investigate.
Does temporary protection finish the job?
No. It is intended to limit exposure while the permanent repair plan is established. Confirm the area covered, its limitations and the remaining repair work.
Can roofing and siding damage be addressed together?

Tell us about every affected exterior area. The estimate should identify each service, its materials and the connections between repairs, with interior work or other separate services clearly identified.

sections.title: Energy-Efficient Windows: What the Ratings Mean

children.text: Compare energy ratings for the exact window, glazing package and configuration included in your estimate. The National Fenestration Rating Council (NFRC) label provides standardized information that can help homeowners compare products.

U-factor describes how readily heat moves through a window assembly. Lower numbers indicate less heat transfer under the standardized test conditions. It does not predict an exact reduction in your utility bill.

SHGC describes how much solar heat passes through the window. The appropriate value depends partly on orientation, shading and how the room is used. A single number is not automatically right for every side of the house.
VT describes the amount of visible light passing through the product. Tinting, coatings and glass choices can affect daylight and appearance as well as thermal performance.

Ask for the actual product specifications, glass package and rating information in writing. Energy savings depend on the entire home, existing windows, installation and occupant behavior. A rating alone does not establish the savings for your house.

sections.title: The Opening, Flashing and Finishing Work

children.text: An insert replacement may retain sound portions of the existing frame. That can reduce disturbance to interior finishes when the existing opening is square, stable and suitable for the selected unit. It is not appropriate for every home.

Fuller removal exposes more of the opening and may be necessary when the frame is deteriorated, distorted or affected by water. The proposal should explain which parts remain, which are removed and how hidden damage will be handled if it is discovered. Neither approach should be selected only because it is easier to quote.

The crew should protect surrounding areas, remove the specified materials and check the exposed opening before installing the replacement unit. Concealed deterioration should be documented and approved before additional work proceeds.

A replacement window has to connect properly to the wall. Water reaching the window area needs a way to drain back outside. Sill, jamb and head details depend on the selected window, the wall construction and the installation method.

Finish caulk is not a substitute for a properly planned water-management connection. Ask how the installation will address flashing, perimeter sealing, insulation where appropriate and transitions to siding or exterior trim. The estimate should also state whether interior casing, exterior trim, painting, disposal and cleanup are included.

If you are replacing siding at the same time, coordinating the window-to-wall connections can avoid reworking finished surfaces. Roof King also offers siding services, so those adjoining details can be discussed together.

items.question: Can wind damage a roof without blowing shingles off?

children.text: Yes. Wind can lift shingles and weaken their sealant bonds without leaving a visible gap from the ground. An inspection can help determine whether the affected shingles remain serviceable.

items.question: Do hail dents on gutters mean my roof needs replacement?

children.text: No. Dents are evidence that hail struck a surface, but the roof covering needs its own assessment. Metal marks alone do not establish that every shingle has functional damage.

items.question: How soon should I schedule a roof inspection after a storm?

children.text: Arrange an inspection reasonably promptly if you see missing shingles, loose flashing, fallen debris or interior water staining. If there is an immediate safety hazard, address that first.

items.question: Will homeowners insurance pay for storm damage roof repairs?

children.text: It may, depending on your policy and the cause and extent of the damage. The insurance company determines coverage. Roof King can document roofing conditions and provide a repair or replacement estimate.

items.question: Can Roof King repair storm-damaged siding and gutters too?

children.text: Roof King offers roofing, siding and gutter services. The assessment can identify related exterior damage so the appropriate work is described and priced separately.

items.question: Does a small roof leak mean I need a new roof?

children.text: Not necessarily. A localized flashing or shingle problem may be repairable. Repeated leaks, widespread storm damage or deteriorated roofing materials can change the recommendation.

items.question: Is a free inspection the same as an insurance adjustment?

children.text: No. A roofing inspection addresses the condition of the roof and possible construction work. Your insurer evaluates coverage under the policy.

cards.title: Signs of Wind Damage on a Residential Roof

children.text: Wind commonly affects roof edges, ridges and areas around chimneys or other projections. Some damage is visible from the yard; other conditions require a trained inspection.
Missing, displaced or creased shingles.
Lifted shingles or broken sealant bonds that may be difficult to see from the ground.
Loose ridge caps, drip edge or flashing around chimneys, skylights and vents.
Shingle pieces, nails or roofing debris found in the yard.
Gutters or siding pulled loose by wind or falling limbs.
A shingle that has lifted and settled back into place may still have a compromised seal. That is one reason a roof can leak during the next storm even when no shingles appear to be missing.

cards.title: What Hail Damage Looks Like

children.text: Hail can affect shingles, roof vents, soft-metal flashing and gutters. Dents in metal are worth documenting, but they do not by themselves prove that every nearby shingle is damaged. Hail size, roof age, material and the angle of impact all matter.

On asphalt shingles, an inspector looks for impact-related surface changes and distinguishes them from normal wear, blistering, foot traffic or older damage. A proper assessment explains the location and significance of the findings rather than relying on a single close-up photo.
If you see dented gutters, granules near downspouts or marks on roof accessories after a hailstorm, report them when requesting the inspection. Avoid rubbing, lifting or testing shingles yourself.

Fallen limbs may puncture roofing or damage the decking underneath. If a tree is resting on the house, leave removal and structural evaluation to qualified professionals. The roof repair estimate should account for any damage discovered after the obstruction is safely removed.

items.question: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

children.text: Usually, yes. The City of Columbus requires a permit and plan review for a new deck. The only exception is a deck that is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade, not attached to the house and not serving the required exit door. Decks over 169 square feet also need zoning approval. Suburbs set their own rules.

items.question: Does my deck need a railing?

children.text: In Columbus, a deck more than 30 inches above grade (measured 3 feet out from the edge) needs a 36- inch guard. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.

items.question: Is composite decking hotter than wood?

children.text: Composite gets hot in direct sun, and darker colors run hotter. Trex's heat-mitigating boards, such as Transcend Lineage and certain Select and Enhance colors, stay cooler than its original boards but can still get hot on summer afternoons.

items.question: Can I stain or paint a Trex deck?

children.text: Current Trex decking is designed for cleaning rather than periodic staining. Painting or staining can affect fade-and-stain coverage, and sanding can damage the surface. Identify the product line and follow its specific care instructions; older composite lines have different cleaning limits.

items.question: Can I put a fire pit on a composite deck?

children.text: Not a wood-burning one sitting directly on the boards. Trex notes its decking can soften at temperatures as low as 176°F. Check the product's instructions before placing any heat source on the deck.

items.question: Which warranty covers my deck?

children.text: Manufacturer product coverage and Roof King’s five-year workmanship coverage are separate. Trex residential decking terms vary by line, generally from 25 to 50 years. Your written estimate identifies the selected line and applicable coverage; keep both warranty documents with the project records.

items.question: Do you work on decks outside Columbus?

children.text: Yes, we serve communities across central Ohio. See our
service areas
. Permit rules change at city limits, so your estimate should say which building department applies.

items.question: How do I get a deck estimate?

children.text: Call (614) 490-0123 or book a time online. Estimates are free. Tell us whether you're planning a new deck or have an existing one to repair, resurface or refinish.

Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

Usually, yes. The City of Columbus requires a permit and plan review for a new deck. The only exception is a deck that is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade, not attached to the house and not serving the required exit door. Decks over 169 square feet also need zoning approval. Suburbs set their own rules.
Does my deck need a railing?

In Columbus, a deck more than 30 inches above grade (measured 3 feet out from the edge) needs a 36- inch guard. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.
Is composite decking hotter than wood?

Composite gets hot in direct sun, and darker colors run hotter. Trex's heat-mitigating boards, such as Transcend Lineage and certain Select and Enhance colors, stay cooler than its original boards but can still get hot on summer afternoons.
Can I stain or paint a Trex deck?

Current Trex decking is designed for cleaning rather than periodic staining. Painting or staining can affect fade-and-stain coverage, and sanding can damage the surface. Identify the product line and follow its specific care instructions; older composite lines have different cleaning limits.
Can I put a fire pit on a composite deck?
Not a wood-burning one sitting directly on the boards. Trex notes its decking can soften at temperatures as low as 176°F. Check the product's instructions before placing any heat source on the deck.
Which warranty covers my deck?

Manufacturer product coverage and Roof King’s five-year workmanship coverage are separate. Trex residential decking terms vary by line, generally from 25 to 50 years. Your written estimate identifies the selected line and applicable coverage; keep both warranty documents with the project records.
Do you work on decks outside Columbus?
Yes, we serve communities across central Ohio. See our service areas. Permit rules change at city limits, so your estimate should say which building department applies.
How do I get a deck estimate?
Call (614) 490-0123 or book a time online. Estimates are free. Tell us whether you're planning a new deck or have an existing one to repair, resurface or refinish.
Tell us about the deck you want or the problem with your existing deck. We assess the structure and materials, discuss the options and prepare a free written estimate.

children.text: Six questions narrow the choice for most decks. Bring your answers to the inspection.

cards.title: The View
cards.description: Decide how much you want to see through the railing when you're sitting down.
cards.summary: Which Infill Keeps The View Open?

children.text: Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass give the clearest view at seated eye level. Framed glass and Rod Rail are close behind. Rods and cables read as horizontal lines. Balusters and mesh give more privacy and a more traditional look. Glass panels need regular cleaning to stay clear.

cards.title: Maintenance
cards.description: Each railing material needs different care, and the connections matter as much as the finish.

children.text: Aluminum, steel, composite, glass and cable infill each call for different surface care. Check for loose caps, damaged connectors and post movement after storms or heavy use, and keep the exact railing model on record so replacement parts and cleaning methods match. A painted or stained wood railing also needs refinishing as its coating wears. Our
deck refinishing
page covers wood upkeep. If you keep a wood deck, a Trex railing can still go on it. See tab 4.

cards.title: Budget
cards.description: The railing line, the number of stair runs and the post count drive the cost more than the deck's size does.

children.text: Line and infill: Trex describes Enhance as budget-friendly and Select T-Rail as near vinyl in cost. Signature glass and cable sit at the other end. Linear feet of railing, plus the count of corners, gates and stair sections. Posts and blocking: every guard post needs a solid attachment to the framing. Lighting added to posts and stairs, and any repairs found at the inspection.

cards.title: Code
cards.description: If the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, Columbus requires a guard at least 36 inches high.
cards.summary: The Rules A Railing Has To Meet

children.text: City of Columbus BZS memo CIC #23 quotes Residential Code of Ohio 312.1. It requires "a 36 inch high guardrail" on decks where the grade is more than 30 inches below the deck surface, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The American Wood Council's deck guide adds that openings must not let a 4-inch sphere pass, including under built-in benches. It also recommends measuring guard height from a fixed seat rather than the deck surface. Trex Select comes in 36- and 42- inch heights.

cards.title: Stairs
cards.description: Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail.
cards.summary: Handrail And Step Rules In Columbus

children.text: Handrail 34 to 38 inches high, on at least one side, when there are 4 or more risers (RCO 311.7.7). Risers no more than 8¼ inches. Treads at least 9 inches deep. Open risers must not pass a 4-inch sphere (RCO 311.7.4). The AWC guide calls for a graspable handrail that runs continuously over the full flight.

cards.title: Matching The House
cards.description: Pick the rail color against the trim, windows and door frames, not the deck boards alone.

children.text: Rail and post colors vary by line, and boards that have weathered won't match a new sample exactly. Compare real samples outside, next to your siding and trim. The
deck visualizer
helps you try combinations before the inspection.

items.title: Lighting, Fasteners, Fascia And Drainage
items.description: These four Trex accessories are planned before the boards go down. Wiring, clips, trim and drainage are much harder to add once the deck is closed in.

children.text: These four Trex accessories are planned before the boards go down. Wiring, clips, trim and drainage are much harder to add once the deck is closed in.

cards.title: Deck And Stair Lighting
cards.description: Decide where light is needed (steps, posts, under the rail) before posts are sleeved.

children.text: Trex says its lights run on 24 volts rather than 120-volt household current, use LEDs, and plug into a standard outlet through a transformer. A photocell timer runs the lights dusk to dawn or for 2, 4 or up to 10 hours, and a remote dimmer is available. Trex lists a 5-year limited warranty on its lights and transformers. Accent lights don't replace the stair light the code expects. The AWC guide (citing IRC R303.7) calls for a light source at the top landing that lights all the stairs, switched from inside the house. Motion or timer switches are acceptable.

cards.title: Hidden Or Face Fastening
cards.description: Grooved boards take hidden clips. Square-edge boards and fascia take screws and plugs.
cards.summary: Why The Board Decides The Fastener

children.text: Trex's Universal Hidden Fastener is self-gapping and comes with a stainless steel screw already installed. Clips only work on boards with grooved edges. Stair treads, picture-frame borders and fascia use color-matched composite screws and plugs instead. The estimate names which fastener goes where.

cards.title: Fascia And Finished Edges
cards.description: Fascia hides the framing at the rim and stairs.

children.text: Trex makes fascia in 1×8 and 1×12 boards, 12 feet long, and says it offers matching fascia for every Trex decking color plus Universal White. It needs no sanding, staining or painting. It's a trim board fastened over the rim, so the rim behind it still has to be sound.

cards.title: Under-Deck Drainage
cards.description: RainEscape makes the space under an elevated deck usable.

children.text: Trex says RainEscape keeps rain, spills and snowmelt from dripping through the boards and lets you create a dry patio or storage area below. It comes in brown or black, and Trex lists a 25-year warranty. It sits below the boards, so routing is settled before the walking surface goes down. On an existing deck, ask whether boards need to come up.

cards.title: Trex DeckLighting
cards.description: Deck lighting helps define steps, railings and the edges of outdoor living areas after dark. Plan fixture locations, wiring access and the power supply before enclosing posts or finishing the underside of the deck.
cards.label: Explore Trex DeckLighting

cards.title: Trex Hideaway Fasteners
cards.description: Hideaway includes fastening choices for grooved decking, face-fastened boards and fascia. Hidden clips attach at the board edges; screws and plugs address other locations. Selecting the fastener by board profile and application avoids using a fascia connection in the walking surface.
cards.label: Explore Trex Hideaway Fasteners

cards.title: Trex Fascia
cards.description: Fascia covers the deck rim and gives stair edges a finished appearance. It is a vertical finishing board, not the structural rim joist or a substitute for walking-surface decking. Dedicated fascia fasteners accommodate movement without treating the board like a deck plank.
cards.label: Explore Trex Fascia

cards.title: Trex RainEscape
cards.description: RainEscape collects water below the deck boards and directs it away through troughs and downspouts. It is most useful when you want to use the space under an elevated deck. Drainage routing and access need to be resolved before the walking surface is installed.
cards.label: Explore Trex RainEscape

items.description: Many Columbus projects keep the deck and replace the railing, add stair lights or close in the underside. Whether that works depends on what's holding the railing, not on the boards you can see.

cards.title: New Railing On A Wood Deck
cards.description: Trex composite railings mount over wood framing.

children.text: Trex Select post sleeves slide over a 4×4 pressure-treated post. Trex says Select railings go over the deck frame or on the inside of the rim joist. Notched posts and posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist are not allowed. Blocking must be added for extra strength. Aluminum lines use their own post mounts, so we check the framing under each post before ordering.

cards.title: Posts And The Rim
cards.description: Guard posts are only as strong as the joist they bolt to.
cards.summary: What The AWC Guide Calls For

children.text: The American Wood Council's deck guide calls for guard posts of at least 4×4 attached to joists or rim joists of at least 2×8, with hold-down anchors rated for at least 1,800 pounds for a 36-inch guard. It notes that the IRC requires guards to resist a 200-pound load in any direction. Soft or split rim boards are repaired before a new railing goes on. That work is priced on its own line. See
deck repair

cards.title: Ledger And House Connection
cards.description: A railing upgrade is a good time to check how the deck is attached.
cards.summary: What The Ohio Code Requires At The House

children.text: CIC #23 quotes RCO 502.2.2: attached decks must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and the attachment can't rely on toenails or nails subject to withdrawal. It also quotes RCO 703.8, which requires corrosion-resistant flashing where a deck meets a wood-frame wall. If the ledger or flashing is failing, fixing it comes before new railing.

cards.title: Moving Or Adding Stairs
cards.description: A new stair changes the route into the yard and needs its own landing and footing.

children.text: Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to the exit route between the door and the yard, including decks, landings and stairs. Landings and stairs 30 inches or less above grade can be issued a simpler minor permit that needs a final inspection when the work is done. Plan the new stair position around doors, furniture and the path into the yard.

cards.title: When A New Railing Isn't The Answer
cards.description: If the posts, rim and ledger all need work, a full rebuild can cost about the same as repairs plus a new railing.

children.text: Replacement vs. repair plus railing Compare a repair-plus-railing estimate with a rebuild before deciding. See
deck replacement
for rebuilding on the same footprint, or
new deck installation
when the railing is part of a new build.

items.question: How high does a deck railing have to be in Columbus?

children.text: At least 36 inches, when the deck surface is more than 30 inches above the ground measured 3 feet out from the edge. That's Residential Code of Ohio 312.1, as quoted in the City of Columbus deck memo (CIC #23). Stair handrails are 34 to 38 inches high when there are four or more risers.

items.question: Do I need a permit to replace my deck railing?

children.text: Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to decks, landings and stairs that form the exit route from a door, and a permit with plan review to build a deck. Whether a same-for-same railing swap needs one depends on the work, so call Columbus Building and Zoning Services or ask us to check before work starts.

items.question: Can I put a Trex railing on my wood deck?

children.text: Usually, yes. Trex Select post sleeves fit over 4×4 pressure-treated posts. Trex requires added blocking and doesn't allow notched posts or posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist. We check the posts and rim first, and any repairs are listed separately.

items.question: Which railing gives the best view?

children.text: Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass keep the view most open, with framed glass and Rod Rail close behind. Glass needs cleaning to stay clear. Balusters and mesh give more privacy.

items.question: What's the difference between Trex Signature, Transcend, Select and Enhance?

children.text: Signature is aluminum with baluster, glass, mesh, rod and cable options. Transcend is a substantial composite rail. Select offers composite and metal options, and Enhance is Trex's value line in composite or steel. Trex lists warranties of 50 years for Signature, 35 for Transcend, 25 for most Select and for Enhance composite, and 15 for Enhance steel.

items.question: Can I add lighting to an existing deck?

children.text: Often, yes. Trex says post cap and stair riser lights can be added to an existing deck, while under-rail lights go in with the railing. The lights run on 24 volts through a plug-in transformer, so we plan the wire route and the outlet location.

items.question: Is under-deck drainage worth it?

children.text: It is if you want to use the space below an upper deck as a dry patio or for storage. Trex RainEscape catches water under the boards and carries it to downspouts. It goes in below the boards, so it's easiest during a new deck or a resurfacing.

items.question: Do hidden fasteners work on every board?

children.text: No. Hidden clips need boards with grooved edges. Square-edge boards, stair treads and fascia use color-matched screws and plugs. Your estimate states which fastener is used where.

Matching The House

Rail and post colors vary by line, and boards that have weathered won't match a new sample exactly. Compare real samples outside, next to your siding and trim. The deck visualizer helps you try combinations before the inspection.
Lighting, Fasteners, Fascia And Drainage
These four Trex accessories are planned before the boards go down. Wiring, clips, trim and drainage are much harder to add once the deck is closed in.
Deck And Stair Lighting

Trex says its lights run on 24 volts rather than 120-volt household current, use LEDs, and plug into a standard outlet through a transformer. A photocell timer runs the lights dusk to dawn or for 2, 4 or up to 10 hours, and a remote dimmer is available. Trex lists a 5-year limited warranty on its lights and transformers. Accent lights don't replace the stair light the code expects. The AWC guide (citing IRC R303.7) calls for a light source at the top landing that lights all the stairs, switched from inside the house. Motion or timer switches are acceptable.
Hidden Or Face Fastening

Trex's Universal Hidden Fastener is self-gapping and comes with a stainless steel screw already installed. Clips only work on boards with grooved edges. Stair treads, picture-frame borders and fascia use color-matched composite screws and plugs instead. The estimate names which fastener goes where.
Fascia And Finished Edges

Trex makes fascia in 1×8 and 1×12 boards, 12 feet long, and says it offers matching fascia for every Trex decking color plus Universal White. It needs no sanding, staining or painting. It's a trim board fastened over the rim, so the rim behind it still has to be sound.
Under-Deck Drainage

Trex says RainEscape keeps rain, spills and snowmelt from dripping through the boards and lets you create a dry patio or storage area below. It comes in brown or black, and Trex lists a 25-year warranty. It sits below the boards, so routing is settled before the walking surface goes down. On an existing deck, ask whether boards need to come up.

Adding To An Existing Deck
Many Columbus projects keep the deck and replace the railing, add stair lights or close in the underside. Whether that works depends on what's holding the railing, not on the boards you can see.
New Railing On A Wood Deck

Trex Select post sleeves slide over a 4×4 pressure-treated post. Trex says Select railings go over the deck frame or on the inside of the rim joist. Notched posts and posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist are not allowed. Blocking must be added for extra strength. Aluminum lines use their own post mounts, so we check the framing under each post before ordering.
Posts And The Rim

The American Wood Council's deck guide calls for guard posts of at least 4×4 attached to joists or rim joists of at least 2×8, with hold-down anchors rated for at least 1,800 pounds for a 36-inch guard. It notes that the IRC requires guards to resist a 200-pound load in any direction. Soft or split rim boards are repaired before a new railing goes on. That work is priced on its own line. See deck repair.
Ledger And House Connection

CIC #23 quotes RCO 502.2.2: attached decks must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and the attachment can't rely on toenails or nails subject to withdrawal. It also quotes RCO 703.8, which requires corrosion-resistant flashing where a deck meets a wood-frame wall. If the ledger or flashing is failing, fixing it comes before new railing.
Moving Or Adding Stairs

Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to the exit route between the door and the yard, including decks, landings and stairs. Landings and stairs 30 inches or less above grade can be issued a simpler minor permit that needs a final inspection when the work is done. Plan the new stair position around doors, furniture and the path into the yard.
When A New Railing Isn't The Answer

Replacement vs. repair plus railing Compare a repair-plus-railing estimate with a rebuild before deciding. See deck replacement for rebuilding on the same footprint, or new deck installation when the railing is part of a new build.
Railing Height and Guard Rules for Columbus Decks
When a Deck Needs a Guard

Columbus guidance requires a 36-inch guard where the ground is more than 30 inches below the deck surface, measured three feet out from the edge. Railings are planned around the actual deck height, including any perimeter seating and exposed edges.
Openings and Post Attachments Matter

A railing’s appearance does not establish its structural capacity. The selected system needs compatible posts, blocking and connectors, with infill openings and stair details checked against the approved design and applicable requirements.
Stairs Need Their Own Handrail Plan

For four or more risers, Columbus calls for a handrail on at least one side, 34–38 inches above the stair nosings. The handrail, stair framing, guard posts and lighting are coordinated before the finished railing is installed.
What Your Deck Railings and Accessories Estimate Includes
Your written estimate identifies the materials, preparation, construction and cleanup so you can compare the same work between proposals.
Removal and disposal of the agreed railing, stairs or trim
Trex line, color, infill, posts, corners and stair sections
Post blocking, attachment and separately approved supporting repairs
Lighting, wiring route, transformer, fascia and drainage as selected
Permit responsibilities, protection, cleanup and final review
Product coverage and separate workmanship terms
What Changes the Price
Size, height, access, demolition, retained versus new structure, materials, stairs and railing length all affect the price. A deck-area rate alone does not describe those differences.
Additional Repairs and Scheduling

If opening the deck reveals further deterioration, we document it and explain the added repair before it is approved. Material lead times, permit review and weather affect scheduling; the proposal identifies the planned work and responsibilities.
How high does a deck railing have to be in Columbus?

At least 36 inches, when the deck surface is more than 30 inches above the ground measured 3 feet out from the edge. That's Residential Code of Ohio 312.1, as quoted in the City of Columbus deck memo (CIC #23). Stair handrails are 34 to 38 inches high when there are four or more risers.
Do I need a permit to replace my deck railing?

Columbus requires plan approval and permits for changes to decks, landings and stairs that form the exit route from a door, and a permit with plan review to build a deck. Whether a same-for-same railing swap needs one depends on the work, so call Columbus Building and Zoning Services or ask us to check before work starts.
Can I put a Trex railing on my wood deck?

Usually, yes. Trex Select post sleeves fit over 4×4 pressure-treated posts. Trex requires added blocking and doesn't allow notched posts or posts bolted to the outside of the rim joist. We check the posts and rim first, and any repairs are listed separately.
Which railing gives the best view?
Cable (Signature X-Series) and frameless glass keep the view most open, with framed glass and Rod Rail close behind. Glass needs cleaning to stay clear. Balusters and mesh give more privacy.
What's the difference between Trex Signature, Transcend, Select and Enhance?

Signature is aluminum with baluster, glass, mesh, rod and cable options. Transcend is a substantial composite rail. Select offers composite and metal options, and Enhance is Trex's value line in composite or steel. Trex lists warranties of 50 years for Signature, 35 for Transcend, 25 for most Select and for Enhance composite, and 15 for Enhance steel.
Can I add lighting to an existing deck?

Often, yes. Trex says post cap and stair riser lights can be added to an existing deck, while under-rail lights go in with the railing. The lights run on 24 volts through a plug-in transformer, so we plan the wire route and the outlet location.
Is under-deck drainage worth it?

It is if you want to use the space below an upper deck as a dry patio or for storage. Trex RainEscape catches water under the boards and carries it to downspouts. It goes in below the boards, so it's easiest during a new deck or a resurfacing.
Do hidden fasteners work on every board?
No. Hidden clips need boards with grooved edges. Square-edge boards, stair treads and fascia use color-matched screws and plugs. Your estimate states which fastener is used where.
Tell us about the deck you want or the problem with your existing deck. We assess the structure and materials, discuss the options and prepare a free written estimate.

items.title: Size And Layout
items.description: Size a deck from the activities it has to hold, then check the result against the City's thresholds. A few square feet can change which approvals you need.

children.text: Size a deck from the activities it has to hold, then check the result against the City's thresholds. A few square feet can change which approvals you need.

cards.title: Furniture First, Then The Footprint
cards.description: Lay out the table, chairs or lounge seating you'll actually use, then keep a clear walking route from the door to the stairs.

children.text: Measure the furniture with chairs pulled out, not pushed in. Keep the door swing and the stair top clear of seating. Separate zones, such as dining and lounging, can be divided by a landing or a change in level.

cards.title: Sizes That Change The Paperwork
cards.description: In Columbus, 169 and 200 square feet are the numbers that matter.

children.text: The City requires zoning approval for any deck over 169 square feet, whatever its height or location. The only deck that skips the building permit and plan review is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade at any point, not attached to the house, and not serving the required exit door. Most attached decks need a permit at any size.

cards.title: Height, Guards And The First Step
cards.description: Deck height decides whether you need guards and how many stairs you'll have.

children.text: A 36-inch guard is required where the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The step down from the door threshold to the deck can be no more than 8¼ inches, provided the door doesn't swing out onto the deck.

cards.title: Stairs And Where They Land
cards.description: Stairs are part of the structure, so plan them early.

children.text: Risers can be no more than 8¼ inches and treads at least 9 inches. Open risers can't pass a 4-inch sphere. Four or more risers need a 34- to 38-inch handrail on at least one side. Stair stringers must bear on footings or a post-supported bearing block, not on a patio slab that isn't founded below frost depth.

cards.title: Multiple Levels
cards.description: Two levels are possible, but they're engineered differently.

children.text: prescriptive deck guide (DCA 6) covers single-level decks only. It notes that stairs between levels add loads its span tables don't consider. A multi-level design is planned and drawn for plan review rather than built from a standard table.

items.title: Attached Or Freestanding
items.description: How a deck connects to the house is the biggest structural decision you'll make. It sets the footings, the fasteners, the flashing and sometimes the permit path.

children.text: How a deck connects to the house is the biggest structural decision you'll make. It sets the footings, the fasteners, the flashing and sometimes the permit path.

cards.title: Ledger-Attached Deck
cards.description: A treated ledger board is bolted to the house's band joist and carries one edge of the deck.

children.text: Works when the band joist is solid framing that bears fully on the foundation or wall below. Siding is removed at the ledger so it can be flashed. The attachment must resist vertical and horizontal movement; toenails or nails that can pull out are not allowed. The AWC prescriptive guide describes lateral hold-downs in at least two places within 2 feet of the deck edges, each rated at 1,500 pounds or more.

cards.title: Non-Ledger Deck (Beam At The House)
cards.description: A second beam on its own posts carries the house-side edge, so the wall doesn't carry the deck's weight.

children.text: The AWC prescriptive guide describes this approach where a ledger isn't allowed: brick, stone or masonry veneer, hollow masonry, or a cantilevered floor or bay window. Those posts sit close to the house. Footings within 5 feet of the foundation must bear at the same depth as the house footing. With a basement next to the deck, that means deep footings.

cards.title: Fully Freestanding Deck
cards.description: A deck that doesn't touch the house at all braces itself and must still meet the code.

children.text: The building code says that if a positive connection to the house can't be verified at inspection, the deck must be self-supporting. A freestanding deck in Columbus can avoid the building permit only if it's 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval still applies above 169 square feet.

cards.title: Which One Fits Your House
cards.description: The wall behind the deck usually decides.

children.text: Vinyl, fiber-cement or wood siding over wood framing: a ledger is often possible once the band joist is confirmed. Brick or stone veneer, a bay window or a cantilevered floor: the code doesn't allow a ledger there, so use a non-ledger beam. A deck in the yard, away from the house: freestanding.

items.title: Footings And Framing
items.description: Footings, posts, beams and joists carry the deck. The design follows the local frost-depth requirements, soil conditions and the loads and support spacing for the selected materials.

cards.title: Footings Below the Local Frost Depth
cards.description: Deck footings must reach suitable bearing soil and the locally required frost depth. The approved design identifies their depth and location.

children.text: Footing design also considers the load, soil, nearby foundations and buried utilities. We identify utility locations before excavation and arrange the required footing inspection before the concrete is placed.

cards.title: Footing Size
cards.description: Footing size is set by the area each post supports and the soil.

children.text: the deck area a post carries (its tributary area) and the soil's bearing capacity. Where weak soil is likely, the building official can require a soils investigation. A bigger deck or a longer beam span means bigger footings, not just more of them.

cards.title: Posts And Beams
cards.description: Post size limits how tall the deck can be.

children.text: DCA 6 uses 6x6 posts as the minimum. The Ohio code ties maximum post height to post size and requires posts to be restrained at the footing with connectors or embedment. Beams need full bearing: at least 1½ inches on wood or metal and 3 inches on concrete.

cards.title: Joist Spacing For The Boards You Choose
cards.description: Joist spacing follows the decking, so choose the boards before the framing is drawn.

children.text: Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when boards run diagonally. The Ohio code ties wood-decking joist spacing to board thickness.

cards.title: Lumber For Columbus Conditions
cards.description: Outdoor framing needs lumber and hardware suited to moisture exposure and the proposed deck design.

children.text: Ground-contact members, cut ends, flashing and connector compatibility are considered together. The estimate identifies the lumber treatment and corrosion-resistant hardware, with the applicable code and product instructions guiding the installation.

items.title: Ledger, Flashing And Fasteners
items.description: At an attached deck, the ledger is where the deck meets the house's wall framing. The code is specific about what goes there.

children.text: At an attached deck, the ledger is where the deck meets the house's wall framing. The code is specific about what goes there.

cards.title: What The Ledger Attaches To
cards.description: A ledger is at least a treated 2x8, fastened to the house's band joist, never to siding, veneer or an overhang.

children.text: The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. The band joist behind it must bear fully on the primary structure. DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and cantilevered floors or bay windows. In those cases a non-ledger beam is used instead (Tab 2).

cards.title: Flashing That Sheds Water
cards.description: Siding comes off at the ledger, and corrosion-resistant flashing laps over it so water can't reach the wall framing.

children.text: Columbus's deck bulletin requires approved corrosion-resistive flashing wherever a deck attaches to wood-frame construction. DCA 6 specifies metal flashing of at least 0.019-inch nominal thickness, or an approved non-metallic material. It also says aluminum shouldn't touch lumber treated with copper-based preservatives. The door threshold above the deck is flashed and sealed against splash and melting snow.

cards.title: Lag Screws And Bolts
cards.description: The ledger connection needs specified structural fasteners and spacing for the deck load and the house framing.

children.text: The drawings identify the fastener type, diameter, spacing and connection details. Ordinary nails and unapproved substitutes cannot replace that connection. Opening the house wall may reveal repairs needed before attachment.

cards.title: Hardware Rated For Treated Lumber
cards.description: Treated lumber corrodes ordinary hardware, so every fastener and connector is rated for it.

children.text: : hot-dip galvanized fasteners to ASTM A153, or stainless steel, silicon bronze or copper joist hangers and post bases in galvanized (G185) or stainless steel fasteners and connectors of the same corrosion-resistant material, so they don't react with each other.

items.question: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

children.text: Almost always. Inside city limits, a deck needs a building permit and plan review. The one exception is a deck of 200 square feet or less that's no more than 30 inches above grade, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval is also required for any deck over 169 square feet.

items.question: How deep do deck footings have to be in Columbus?

children.text: The approved design must account for local frost depth, soil bearing, deck loads and nearby foundations. Footings are inspected before concrete is placed. A shallow block or an old patio slab is not an automatic substitute for a footing designed for the deck.

items.question: Should my deck be attached to the house or freestanding?

children.text: It depends on the wall behind it. A ledger-attached deck needs solid band- joist framing and careful flashing. If a positive connection can't be verified, the code requires the deck to be self-supporting. Brick or stone veneer, bay windows and cantilevered floors need a beam on its own posts instead of a ledger.

items.question: Can a deck ledger go over brick or stone?

children.text: No. The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. AWC's DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and floor overhangs. A non-ledger deck, with an extra beam and posts at the house, is used instead.

items.question: How far apart are the joists for Trex decking?

children.text: Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when the boards run diagonally. Joist spacing is chosen together with the board line.

items.question: Does composite decking get hot?

children.text: Yes. Trex says all decking can get hot in direct sun, especially darker colors. Its SunComfortable colors reduced heat buildup by up to 35 degrees compared with Trex's original boards in lab testing.

items.question: How tall does a deck railing need to be?

children.text: In Columbus, a 36-inch guard is required where the deck is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.

items.question: Can I finance a new deck?

children.text: Ask our team about current financing for eligible deck projects, then review the lender’s rates, repayment schedule and conditions. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

expectedBlocks: A new deck has to work for the way you live and meet the requirements for your address. Roof King plans the door, furniture and stair layout alongside footings, framing and the house connection. Choose Trex, cedar or pressure-treated boards, then identify the construction and finishing details in a free written estimate.
How a New Deck Is Planned and Built
Six decisions shape a new deck. Explore the layout, supporting structure, boards and finishing details before the plans and material order are finalized.
Size And Layout
Size a deck from the activities it has to hold, then check the result against the City's thresholds. A few square feet can change which approvals you need.
Planning and Installation Details
Furniture First, Then The Footprint

Measure the furniture with chairs pulled out, not pushed in. Keep the door swing and the stair top clear of seating. Separate zones, such as dining and lounging, can be divided by a landing or a change in level.
Sizes That Change The Paperwork

The City requires zoning approval for any deck over 169 square feet, whatever its height or location. The only deck that skips the building permit and plan review is 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade at any point, not attached to the house, and not serving the required exit door. Most attached decks need a permit at any size.
Height, Guards And The First Step

A 36-inch guard is required where the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge. The step down from the door threshold to the deck can be no more than 8¼ inches, provided the door doesn't swing out onto the deck.
Stairs And Where They Land

Risers can be no more than 8¼ inches and treads at least 9 inches. Open risers can't pass a 4-inch sphere. Four or more risers need a 34- to 38-inch handrail on at least one side. Stair stringers must bear on footings or a post-supported bearing block, not on a patio slab that isn't founded below frost depth.
Multiple Levels

prescriptive deck guide (DCA 6) covers single-level decks only. It notes that stairs between levels add loads its span tables don't consider. A multi-level design is planned and drawn for plan review rather than built from a standard table.
References for This Topic

Requirements apply to the property’s jurisdiction and the selected product. City of Columbus Deck and Egress Requirements · Ohio Residential Code: Floor and Deck Construction · Trex Installation and Care Resources
Attached Or Freestanding
How a deck connects to the house is the biggest structural decision you'll make. It sets the footings, the fasteners, the flashing and sometimes the permit path.
Ledger-Attached Deck

Works when the band joist is solid framing that bears fully on the foundation or wall below. Siding is removed at the ledger so it can be flashed. The attachment must resist vertical and horizontal movement; toenails or nails that can pull out are not allowed. The AWC prescriptive guide describes lateral hold-downs in at least two places within 2 feet of the deck edges, each rated at 1,500 pounds or more.
Non-Ledger Deck (Beam At The House)

The AWC prescriptive guide describes this approach where a ledger isn't allowed: brick, stone or masonry veneer, hollow masonry, or a cantilevered floor or bay window. Those posts sit close to the house. Footings within 5 feet of the foundation must bear at the same depth as the house footing. With a basement next to the deck, that means deep footings.
Fully Freestanding Deck

The building code says that if a positive connection to the house can't be verified at inspection, the deck must be self-supporting. A freestanding deck in Columbus can avoid the building permit only if it's 200 square feet or less, no more than 30 inches above grade and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval still applies above 169 square feet.
Which One Fits Your House

Vinyl, fiber-cement or wood siding over wood framing: a ledger is often possible once the band joist is confirmed. Brick or stone veneer, a bay window or a cantilevered floor: the code doesn't allow a ledger there, so use a non-ledger beam. A deck in the yard, away from the house: freestanding.
Footings And Framing
Footings, posts, beams and joists carry the deck. The design follows the local frost-depth requirements, soil conditions and the loads and support spacing for the selected materials.
Footings Below the Local Frost Depth

Footing design also considers the load, soil, nearby foundations and buried utilities. We identify utility locations before excavation and arrange the required footing inspection before the concrete is placed.
Footing Size

the deck area a post carries (its tributary area) and the soil's bearing capacity. Where weak soil is likely, the building official can require a soils investigation. A bigger deck or a longer beam span means bigger footings, not just more of them.
Posts And Beams

DCA 6 uses 6x6 posts as the minimum. The Ohio code ties maximum post height to post size and requires posts to be restrained at the footing with connectors or embedment. Beams need full bearing: at least 1½ inches on wood or metal and 3 inches on concrete.
Joist Spacing For The Boards You Choose
Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when boards run diagonally. The Ohio code ties wood-decking joist spacing to board thickness.
Lumber For Columbus Conditions

Ground-contact members, cut ends, flashing and connector compatibility are considered together. The estimate identifies the lumber treatment and corrosion-resistant hardware, with the applicable code and product instructions guiding the installation.
Ledger, Flashing And Fasteners
At an attached deck, the ledger is where the deck meets the house's wall framing. The code is specific about what goes there.
What The Ledger Attaches To

The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. The band joist behind it must bear fully on the primary structure. DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and cantilevered floors or bay windows. In those cases a non-ledger beam is used instead (Tab 2).
Flashing That Sheds Water

Columbus's deck bulletin requires approved corrosion-resistive flashing wherever a deck attaches to wood-frame construction. DCA 6 specifies metal flashing of at least 0.019-inch nominal thickness, or an approved non-metallic material. It also says aluminum shouldn't touch lumber treated with copper-based preservatives. The door threshold above the deck is flashed and sealed against splash and melting snow.
Lag Screws And Bolts

The drawings identify the fastener type, diameter, spacing and connection details. Ordinary nails and unapproved substitutes cannot replace that connection. Opening the house wall may reveal repairs needed before attachment.
Hardware Rated For Treated Lumber

: hot-dip galvanized fasteners to ASTM A153, or stainless steel, silicon bronze or copper joist hangers and post bases in galvanized (G185) or stainless steel fasteners and connectors of the same corrosion-resistant material, so they don't react with each other.
Boards: Trex And Wood
The boards set the look, the upkeep and the joist spacing. Roof King installs Trex composite and PVC lines as well as cedar and pressure-treated wood.
Upkeep
cleanup for Transcend. Wood is cleaned and inspected regularly. A finish is reapplied if you want to keep the color; unfinished cedar weathers to gray. See deck refinishing for wood upkeep.
Heat In The Sun

Some Trex lines and colors include heat-mitigating technology. They can still become hot, especially darker colors. Compare the selected line’s published heat information and plan shade for exposed seating and walking areas.
How Boards Are Fastened
Hidden fastening leaves no visible screw holes in the walking surface. See Trex Hideaway fasteners.

Railings, Lighting And Drainage

Railings, stair lighting and under-deck drainage are easiest to add while the framing is open. Choose them with the deck, not after. Railing styles, stairs and finishing details are covered on deck railings and accessories.
Stair Lighting And Guards Together

Guard posts are bolted into the framing, and lighting wires run through posts and rails. Changing either after framing can mean opening finished work. DCA 6 also calls for a light source at stairways. More options: deck railings and accessories.

Columbus Permits and Inspections for a New Deck
Plan Review Comes Before Construction

Inside Columbus city limits, building a deck normally requires a permit and plan review. The limited exception requires all four conditions: no more than 200 square feet, no more than 30 inches above grade, no house attachment and no service to the required exit door. The proposal identifies who prepares and submits the plans.
Zoning, Overlays and the Property Line

Columbus requires zoning approval for decks over 169 square feet. Setbacks, historic districts and other overlays can affect a design even when a deck is low to the ground. We establish which building department and property restrictions apply before fixing the footprint.
Inspections Before the Work Is Covered

Footings, framing and connections need the inspections specified by the permit. Inspection timing is part of the construction plan so bearing conditions and attachments can be seen before concrete or finished boards conceal them.
What Your New Deck Installation Estimate Includes

What Changes the Price
Size, height, access, demolition, retained versus new structure, materials, stairs and railing length all affect the price. A deck-area rate alone does not describe those differences.
Additional Repairs and Scheduling

If opening the deck reveals further deterioration, we document it and explain the added repair before it is approved. Material lead times, permit review and weather affect scheduling; the proposal identifies the planned work and responsibilities.
Do I need a permit to build a deck in Columbus?

Almost always. Inside city limits, a deck needs a building permit and plan review. The one exception is a deck of 200 square feet or less that's no more than 30 inches above grade, isn't attached to the house and doesn't serve the required exit door. Zoning approval is also required for any deck over 169 square feet.
How deep do deck footings have to be in Columbus?

The approved design must account for local frost depth, soil bearing, deck loads and nearby foundations. Footings are inspected before concrete is placed. A shallow block or an old patio slab is not an automatic substitute for a footing designed for the deck.
Should my deck be attached to the house or freestanding?

It depends on the wall behind it. A ledger-attached deck needs solid band- joist framing and careful flashing. If a positive connection can't be verified, the code requires the deck to be self-supporting. Brick or stone veneer, bay windows and cantilevered floors need a beam on its own posts instead of a ledger.
Can a deck ledger go over brick or stone?

No. The Ohio code doesn't allow a ledger to be supported on stone or masonry veneer. AWC's DCA 6 also prohibits ledgers on hollow masonry and floor overhangs. A non-ledger deck, with an extra beam and posts at the house, is used instead.
How far apart are the joists for Trex decking?
Trex specifies joists no more than 16 inches on center for standard installs and 12 inches when the boards run diagonally. Joist spacing is chosen together with the board line.
Does composite decking get hot?
Yes. Trex says all decking can get hot in direct sun, especially darker colors. Its SunComfortable colors reduced heat buildup by up to 35 degrees compared with Trex's original boards in lab testing.
How tall does a deck railing need to be?

In Columbus, a 36-inch guard is required where the deck is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out. Stairs with four or more risers need a handrail 34 to 38 inches high on at least one side.
Can I finance a new deck?
Ask our team about current financing for eligible deck projects, then review the lender’s rates, repayment schedule and conditions. Financing is subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

items.title: Signs It's Time To Replace
items.description: A deck needs replacing when the problems reach the parts that hold it up: the ledger, posts, footings, joists and railing connections. Damage limited to a few boards or one loose rail is a repair. For that, see [deck repair](/decks/repairs/). Age catches up with decks everywhere. NADRA, the North American Deck and Railing Association, estimates that about 30 million of the 60 million decks in the U.S. have outlived their useful life.
