cards.title: Rot In The Frame, Not Just The Boards
cards.description: Soft wood in the joists, beams or rim means the structure under the surface is failing.

children.text: Joist ends and the tops of joists, where water sits under the boards The ledger and the house rim joist behind it Beam ends and post tops, where wood meets wood Posts at grade, especially where soil or mulch is piled against them Decay in one board is a repair. Decay in several joists or at the ledger usually means rebuilding rather than resurfacing. NADRA's consumer checklist names decaying materials as a key warning sign.

cards.title: A Loose Or Poorly Attached Ledger
cards.description: The ledger is the board that ties the deck to your house.

children.text: ledger looks like Columbus's deck bulletin says an attached deck must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and it can't be attached with toenails or nails that can pull out. The American Wood Council's deck guide (DCA 6) calls for ½-inch lag screws or bolts and corrosion-resistant flashing at the wall. It prohibits fastening a ledger to brick veneer, hollow masonry or a cantilevered floor overhang. Warning signs: A gap opening between the ledger and the house A ledger held with nails only Missing or rusted flashing above the ledger Water stains or soft wood on the house framing below it Fixing a ledger properly means taking up the boards along the house, which is often the point where a full replacement makes more sense.

cards.title: Failing Posts And Footings
cards.description: Posts that lean, rot at the base or sit on blocks at ground level can't be fixed from the deck surface.

children.text: What current practice calls for DCA 6 prescribes posts of at least 6x6. The beam must sit on a notched post or a post cap, not be bolted to the side of the post. Footings bear on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches below grade or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Many older decks have 4x4 posts, beams bolted to the side of the posts, or shallow pier blocks. New boards don't change any of that; correcting it means rebuilding the substructure.

cards.title: Soft, Springy Or Split Boards Across The Deck
cards.description: When the whole surface bounces, cups or splits, the cause is often underneath.

children.text: Boards or joists? One soft board is a repair. Widespread bounce usually traces to joists spaced too far apart for the boards, or to joist tops that have started to decay. Measure the joist spacing before choosing new boards. Composite needs closer spacing than many older wood decks were built with (see tab 3, "Upgrade from wood to Trex composite").

cards.title: Railings And Stairs That Move
cards.description: A rail that shifts when you lean on it is a safety problem, not a cosmetic one.

children.text: What Columbus requires A 36-inch guard wherever the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge A handrail 34–38 inches high on at least one side of any stair with 4 or more risers Stair risers no higher than 8¼ inches, treads at least 9 inches deep, and openings that won't pass a 4-inch sphere DCA 6 calls for guard posts of at least 4x4, bolted to joists or a rim of at least 2x8 and secured with hold-down hardware rated for 1,800 pounds. Railing posts depend on the frame. When the frame is replaced, the railing usually is too. Compare railing systems on
deck railings and accessories

cards.title: Rusted Hardware And Dark Stairs
cards.description: Corroded connectors and unlit steps are on NADRA's short list of deck warning signs.

children.text: Why the metal matters DCA 6 requires hot-dip galvanized or stainless steel fasteners and connectors with preservative-treated lumber. Rusted joist hangers, ledger bolts and post bases lose capacity long before they break. DCA 6 also calls for a light at the top landing that lights every stair, switched from inside the house. A replacement is the time to correct both.

items.tabLabel: Resurface Or Replace The Whole Deck
items.title: Resurface Or Replace The Whole Deck
items.description: Roof King offers both resurfacing and full replacement. Resurfacing keeps the existing frame and replaces what you walk on and touch: the boards, and usually the railings, stair treads and fascia. Full replacement removes the deck and rebuilds the structure. The frame decides which one fits your deck, not the condition of the old boards. Fixing a few named parts on a deck that stays is [deck repair](/decks/repairs/).

cards.title: When Resurfacing Makes Sense
cards.description: A sound, well-connected frame can carry a new surface for years.

children.text: Resurfacing usually works when… Joists, beams and ledger are dry and solid, with no decay at the ends or along the ledger The ledger is bolted to the house and flashed Posts and footings meet the practice described in tab 1 Joist spacing suits the new boards, or can be corrected by adding joists You're happy with the current size, shape and stair location The estimate names every retained component, and any repair found once the old boards are off is documented and approved before it's covered.

cards.title: When A Full Replacement Is The Better Call
cards.description: Some problems can only be fixed by taking the deck down.

children.text: Plan a full replacement when… Decay runs through several joists, the beam or the ledger The ledger is nailed, or attached to brick veneer or a floor overhang Posts are undersized or footings are shallow You want a different size, height or shape, or the stairs need to move A changed footprint is a design job. Our
deck installation
page covers layout, access and the supporting construction for a new design.

cards.title: What Resurfacing Still Involves
cards.description: Resurfacing isn't just a board swap.
cards.summary: With The Old Boards Off Removing The

children.text: old surface exposes the joist tops, hangers and ledger for the first time in years. That's when the frame is checked closely. Rusted hardware is replaced, weak joists are reinforced or replaced, and added joists go in if the new boards need closer spacing. Railings and stairs are usually renewed at the same time, because their posts and stringers attach to the frame.

cards.title: Comparing A Resurfacing Price With A Replacement Price
cards.description: They aren't the same job, so they shouldn't be compared on the total alone.

children.text: Ask for both when the frame is borderline A resurfacing proposal should list each retained component and its condition. A replacement proposal should list the new footings, posts, beams, joists and ledger. Where the frame could go either way, ask for both options priced side by side. That way a lower surface-only price isn't mistaken for a rebuilt deck.

cards.title: Upkeep: Composite Vs Wood
cards.description: Composite trades staining for cleaning; wood needs a finish renewed over time.

children.text: What each material asks of you Trex describes soap-and-water cleanup for Transcend. Roof King's product pages list periodic cleaning and no routine wood staining for the Trex lines, with methods that depend on the line. Composite isn't maintenance-free: leaves in the board gaps hold moisture against the frame, and drainage still needs checking. Wood decks need a finish system and renewal, which is our
deck refinishing
service.

cards.title: Can Trex Go On My Existing Frame?
cards.description: Only if the joist spacing and the frame's condition suit it.

children.text: joist spacing first Trex says joists for its decking should generally be no more than 16 inches on center. Diagonal boards need 12 inches, and heavier loads, longer spans or patterns can need 12 inches or less. Older wood decks were sometimes framed at 24 inches. Trex's fix is one new joist between each existing pair. Add-in joists can't make up for decay, a poor ledger or weak footings (see tab 1). Each board also needs its own fasteners and edge details for the line selected.

cards.title: Heat In Summer Sun
cards.description: Deck boards can become hot in direct sun. Color, shade and the selected product line affect surface temperature.

children.text: Some Trex lines and colors include heat-mitigating technology. They can still become hot, especially darker colors. Compare the selected line’s published heat information and plan shade for exposed seating and walking areas.

cards.title: Two Warranties, Two Jobs
cards.description: The board warranty and the installation warranty cover different things.

children.text: covers what Trex's limited residential warranties cover the product and differ by line. Transcend and Transcend Lineage carry 50-year limited residential warranties; Select carries a 35-year and Enhance a 25-year limited residential fade-and-stain warranty. Roof King's 5-year workmanship warranty covers our installation and is separate from the manufacturer's terms. Keep both documents with your project records.

expectedBlocks: Worn boards can hide a sound frame or a structure that needs rebuilding. Roof King checks the ledger, joists, posts and footings before recommending resurfacing or full deck replacement in Columbus. The estimate names what stays, what comes off and how the new boards, railings and stairs are built.
Decide What Stays and What Needs Replacing
Use the condition of the structure to compare resurfacing with a rebuild, then consider layout improvements and the materials for the new surface.
Signs It's Time To Replace

A deck needs replacing when the problems reach the parts that hold it up: the ledger, posts, footings, joists and railing connections. Damage limited to a few boards or one loose rail is a repair. For that, see deck repair. Age catches up with decks everywhere. NADRA, the North American Deck and Railing Association, estimates that about 30 million of the 60 million decks in the U.S. have outlived their useful life.
Planning and Installation Details
Rot In The Frame, Not Just The Boards

Joist ends and the tops of joists, where water sits under the boards The ledger and the house rim joist behind it Beam ends and post tops, where wood meets wood Posts at grade, especially where soil or mulch is piled against them Decay in one board is a repair. Decay in several joists or at the ledger usually means rebuilding rather than resurfacing. NADRA's consumer checklist names decaying materials as a key warning sign.
A Loose Or Poorly Attached Ledger

ledger looks like Columbus's deck bulletin says an attached deck must resist both vertical and horizontal movement, and it can't be attached with toenails or nails that can pull out. The American Wood Council's deck guide (DCA 6) calls for ½-inch lag screws or bolts and corrosion-resistant flashing at the wall. It prohibits fastening a ledger to brick veneer, hollow masonry or a cantilevered floor overhang. Warning signs: A gap opening between the ledger and the house A ledger held with nails only Missing or rusted flashing above the ledger Water stains or soft wood on the house framing below it Fixing a ledger properly means taking up the boards along the house, which is often the point where a full replacement makes more sense.
Failing Posts And Footings

What current practice calls for DCA 6 prescribes posts of at least 6x6. The beam must sit on a notched post or a post cap, not be bolted to the side of the post. Footings bear on undisturbed soil at least 12 inches below grade or below the frost line, whichever is deeper. Many older decks have 4x4 posts, beams bolted to the side of the posts, or shallow pier blocks. New boards don't change any of that; correcting it means rebuilding the substructure.
Soft, Springy Or Split Boards Across The Deck

Boards or joists? One soft board is a repair. Widespread bounce usually traces to joists spaced too far apart for the boards, or to joist tops that have started to decay. Measure the joist spacing before choosing new boards. Composite needs closer spacing than many older wood decks were built with (see tab 3, "Upgrade from wood to Trex composite").
Railings And Stairs That Move

What Columbus requires A 36-inch guard wherever the deck surface is more than 30 inches above grade, measured 3 feet out from the edge A handrail 34–38 inches high on at least one side of any stair with 4 or more risers Stair risers no higher than 8¼ inches, treads at least 9 inches deep, and openings that won't pass a 4-inch sphere DCA 6 calls for guard posts of at least 4x4, bolted to joists or a rim of at least 2x8 and secured with hold-down hardware rated for 1,800 pounds. Railing posts depend on the frame. When the frame is replaced, the railing usually is too. Compare railing systems on deck railings and accessories.
Rusted Hardware And Dark Stairs

Why the metal matters DCA 6 requires hot-dip galvanized or stainless steel fasteners and connectors with preservative-treated lumber. Rusted joist hangers, ledger bolts and post bases lose capacity long before they break. DCA 6 also calls for a light at the top landing that lights every stair, switched from inside the house. A replacement is the time to correct both.
References for This Topic

Requirements apply to the property’s jurisdiction and the selected product. City of Columbus Deck and Egress Requirements · Ohio Residential Code: Floor and Deck Construction · Trex Installation and Care Resources
Resurface Or Replace The Whole Deck

Roof King offers both resurfacing and full replacement. Resurfacing keeps the existing frame and replaces what you walk on and touch: the boards, and usually the railings, stair treads and fascia. Full replacement removes the deck and rebuilds the structure. The frame decides which one fits your deck, not the condition of the old boards. Fixing a few named parts on a deck that stays is deck repair.
Compare the Work Included
When Resurfacing Makes Sense

Resurfacing usually works when… Joists, beams and ledger are dry and solid, with no decay at the ends or along the ledger The ledger is bolted to the house and flashed Posts and footings meet the practice described in tab 1 Joist spacing suits the new boards, or can be corrected by adding joists You're happy with the current size, shape and stair location The estimate names every retained component, and any repair found once the old boards are off is documented and approved before it's covered.
When A Full Replacement Is The Better Call

Plan a full replacement when… Decay runs through several joists, the beam or the ledger The ledger is nailed, or attached to brick veneer or a floor overhang Posts are undersized or footings are shallow You want a different size, height or shape, or the stairs need to move A changed footprint is a design job. Our deck installation page covers layout, access and the supporting construction for a new design.
What Resurfacing Still Involves

old surface exposes the joist tops, hangers and ledger for the first time in years. That's when the frame is checked closely. Rusted hardware is replaced, weak joists are reinforced or replaced, and added joists go in if the new boards need closer spacing. Railings and stairs are usually renewed at the same time, because their posts and stringers attach to the frame.
Comparing A Resurfacing Price With A Replacement Price

Ask for both when the frame is borderline A resurfacing proposal should list each retained component and its condition. A replacement proposal should list the new footings, posts, beams, joists and ledger. Where the frame could go either way, ask for both options priced side by side. That way a lower surface-only price isn't mistaken for a rebuilt deck.
Upgrade From Wood To Trex Composite

A replacement is the best time to change materials, because the frame is open and can be set up for the new boards. Roof King's product library covers Trex decking, railing and accessories, along with cedar and pressure-treated wood for homeowners who want to stay with wood.
Upkeep: Composite Vs Wood

What each material asks of you Trex describes soap-and-water cleanup for Transcend. Roof King's product pages list periodic cleaning and no routine wood staining for the Trex lines, with methods that depend on the line. Composite isn't maintenance-free: leaves in the board gaps hold moisture against the frame, and drainage still needs checking. Wood decks need a finish system and renewal, which is our deck refinishing service.
Can Trex Go On My Existing Frame?

joist spacing first Trex says joists for its decking should generally be no more than 16 inches on center. Diagonal boards need 12 inches, and heavier loads, longer spans or patterns can need 12 inches or less. Older wood decks were sometimes framed at 24 inches. Trex's fix is one new joist between each existing pair. Add-in joists can't make up for decay, a poor ledger or weak footings (see tab 1). Each board also needs its own fasteners and edge details for the line selected.
Heat In Summer Sun

Some Trex lines and colors include heat-mitigating technology. They can still become hot, especially darker colors. Compare the selected line’s published heat information and plan shade for exposed seating and walking areas.
Two Warranties, Two Jobs

covers what Trex's limited residential warranties cover the product and differ by line. Transcend and Transcend Lineage carry 50-year limited residential warranties; Select carries a 35-year and Enhance a 25-year limited residential fade-and-stain warranty. Roof King's 5-year workmanship warranty covers our installation and is separate from the manufacturer's terms. Keep both documents with your project records.

cards.title: The Splash Test
cards.description: Sprinkle a little water on a few boards in full sun and in shade.

children.text: Water beads and runs off: the finish is still repelling water. Water darkens the wood and soaks in: the finish has worn through, and the deck is due for refinishing. The Forest Products Laboratory describes this test for water-repellent finishes, and Cabot uses the same check for stains: if the stain still repels water, it's still working. On a new deck, the same test tells you when the wood is ready to take stain. If the droplets soak in, it can be stained.

cards.title: Gray Or Blotchy Boards
cards.description: Gray is weathered wood, not dirt.
cards.summary: What's Happening USDA Forest Products Laboratory

children.text: research explains that unfinished wood outdoors loses its surface color and picks up mildew, so all species eventually turn gray. It treats graying on a finished deck as a sign the finish needs renewing. Cleaning removes the gray layer before new stain goes on.

cards.title: Rough, Checked Or Splintering Boards
cards.description: Small cracks along the grain and raised fibers mean the surface is drying out and wearing.

children.text: Surface checks are common on deck boards because the sun dries the top of the board faster than the rest. Sanding can take the loose, weathered fibers off before a new finish. items.title: Stain Types
items.description: Deck stains run from nearly clear to fully opaque. More pigment hides more of the wood. On a surface people walk on, though, more pigment also means more film that can wear and peel.

children.text: Deck stains run from nearly clear to fully opaque. More pigment hides more of the wood. On a surface people walk on, though, more pigment also means more film that can wear and peel.

cards.title: Clear And Toned (Transparent) Finishes
cards.description: Show the most grain and color of the wood.

children.text: Newer or well-kept cedar and decks where you want the natural wood to show Penetrating water-repellent finishes are one of the finish types the Forest Products Laboratory recommends for fully exposed decks. They also wear fastest: FPL notes that a water-repellent preservative used as a natural finish may last only 1 to 2 years. Renewing it is simple: clean, then recoat.

cards.title: Semi-Transparent Stain
cards.description: Adds color while the grain still shows through.

children.text: Most weathered wood decks, including pressure-treated pine Penetrating semi-transparent stains soak into the wood instead of forming a film, so they don't blister or peel. When it's time to recoat, heavy scraping and sanding usually aren't needed. They have to soak in to work. Excess that sits on the surface is wiped off rather than left to form shiny spots.

cards.title: Semi-Solid Stain
cards.description: Masks most of the grain but keeps some texture.
cards.summary: Best For Decks With Mismatched Boards Or

children.text: uneven weathering where you still want some texture to show.

cards.title: Solid-Color Stain
cards.description: Hides the grain completely and looks close to paint.

children.text: Solid-color stains form a film much like paint. The Forest Products Laboratory warns that, unless a product is specially formulated for decks, they shouldn't be used on horizontal surfaces because they lack abrasion resistance and tend to flake. Going back from a solid stain to a semi-transparent one means removing the old film, because a penetrating stain can't soak through it. items.question: How do I know if my deck needs refinishing?

children.text: Splash some water on the boards. If it beads up, the finish is still working. If the wood darkens and soaks it up, or the deck has turned gray, it's time to refinish. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory and stain maker Cabot both describe this check.

items.question: Can a new stain go over the old one?

children.text: Sometimes. A sound penetrating stain can often be cleaned and recoated with a compatible product. A peeling finish, or a solid stain you want to swap for a semi-transparent, has to come off first.

items.question: Is a semi-transparent or solid stain better for a deck?

children.text: For most wood decks, a semi-transparent stain lasts better underfoot because it soaks in instead of forming a film that can peel. A solid stain hides more, but use one only if it's made for deck floors.

items.question: What weather do you need to stain a deck in Columbus?

children.text: The boards must be dry, air and surface temperatures must fit the selected coating’s label, and the forecast must provide its required drying window. Cabot’s general deck guidance gives 50–90°F; individual finishes can have different rain, dew and curing requirements.

items.question: How soon can we use the deck after staining?

children.text: Dry-to-touch, foot-traffic and furniture times can differ. We provide the selected coating’s instructions and allow for the actual weather rather than promising one return-to-use time for every finish.

items.question: Can you stain or sand a Trex deck?

children.text: No. Trex composite gets cleaned, not stained, and Trex doesn't recommend sanding. Its care page gives pressure-washing limits for its newer lines and says not to pressure wash the older ones.

items.question: Do I need a permit to refinish my deck in Columbus?

children.text: The City of Columbus lists exterior painting among the projects that don't need a permit, and staining isn't listed separately. Building a deck does need a permit and plan review. Historic or special districts may need other approvals.

items.question: Will refinishing hide replaced boards and old marks?

children.text: Not completely. New boards, weathering and grain differences can still show after staining. A semi-solid or solid stain evens out color more, and we go over the expected look before work begins.

The boards must be dry, air and surface temperatures must fit the selected coating’s label, and the forecast must provide its required drying window. Cabot’s general deck guidance gives 50–90°F; individual finishes can have different rain, dew and curing requirements.
How soon can we use the deck after staining?

Dry-to-touch, foot-traffic and furniture times can differ. We provide the selected coating’s instructions and allow for the actual weather rather than promising one return-to-use time for every finish.
Can you stain or sand a Trex deck?
No. Trex composite gets cleaned, not stained, and Trex doesn't recommend sanding. Its care page gives pressure-washing limits for its newer lines and says not to pressure wash the older ones.
Do I need a permit to refinish my deck in Columbus?

The City of Columbus lists exterior painting among the projects that don't need a permit, and staining isn't listed separately. Building a deck does need a permit and plan review. Historic or special districts may need other approvals.
Will refinishing hide replaced boards and old marks?
Not completely. New boards, weathering and grain differences can still show after staining. A semi-solid or solid stain evens out color more, and we go over the expected look before work begins.
